homebrew.name: Freshwater (irregular) Pearl
homebrew.desc:
Freshwater (Irregular) Pearl

Freshwater irregular pearl is a distinctive variety of pearl formed within freshwater mollusks and prized for its unusual shapes, soft luster, and natural individuality. Unlike perfectly rounded pearls, irregular freshwater pearls may occur as elongated drops, flattened forms, baroque shapes, twisted contours, rippled surfaces, or entirely unique organic shapes created by the natural growth process. Their coloration ranges from classic white and cream to silver, pink, peach, lavender, golden, and soft gray, with some specimens displaying subtle overtones that shift gently as the pearl is moved beneath the light. Fine examples possess a smooth surface, strong nacre thickness, and a deep orient, producing a soft glow that appears to come from within the pearl rather than from its surface alone.

Jewelers and ornamental artisans value freshwater irregular pearls for their individuality, natural beauty, and versatility. They are commonly fashioned into necklaces, earrings, pendants, bracelets, rings, brooches, hair ornaments, circlets, amulets, decorative inlays, ceremonial objects, and small ornamental carvings. Because each pearl possesses a unique shape, skilled jewelers often design settings specifically around the natural form of the specimen rather than forcing it into uniform patterns. Particularly desirable examples possess thick nacre, strong luster, unusual but harmonious shapes, attractive coloration, and smooth surfaces. Freshwater irregular pearls are frequently mounted in silver, gold, platinum, electrum, bronze, or copper and are especially suited to ornaments depicting waves, shells, fish, mermaids, moons, flowers, and other motifs associated with water, beauty, and natural creation.

In many cultures, freshwater irregular pearls are associated with adaptability, patience, transformation, purity, wisdom, and beauty created through perseverance. Scholars, healers, diplomats, artists, and travelers sometimes carry polished pearls as symbols of patience and the ability to find value in unexpected circumstances. Some traditions view their unusual shapes as reminders that perfection does not require uniformity, while others associate the pearl's formation within a living creature with resilience, protection, and the transformation of hardship into something precious.

Elven traditions may regard freshwater irregular pearls as gifts from rivers, lakes, and hidden waters, valuing their organic forms as expressions of nature's creativity rather than flaws to be corrected. Dwarven artisans may appreciate them as examples of craftsmanship achieved by natural forces over time, comparing their formation to the patient work of a master artisan refining a rare material. River communities and aquatic cultures may exchange irregular pearls as symbols of safe passage, friendship, and harmony with the waters. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though freshwater irregular pearls are favored gemstones for enchanted items concerned with water, healing, diplomacy, transformation, protection, adaptability, or communication with aquatic creatures and spirits.
homebrew.unid:
Pearl

Pearl is an organic gemstone formed when a mollusk deposits successive layers of nacre around an irritant or foreign particle within its shell. Unlike minerals formed through geological processes, pearls are created through biological activity and are composed primarily of calcium carbonate crystals bound together with organic material. Their appearance ranges from pure white and cream to pink, silver, gray, gold, blue, green, black, and many subtle combinations of these colors. The most prized pearls possess a deep, glowing luster known as orient, produced by the interaction of light with the layered structure of the nacre. Pearls may be perfectly round, near-round, oval, button-shaped, drop-shaped, baroque, or irregular, with unusual forms often valued for their individuality. When polished and carefully handled, pearls display a soft satiny glow rather than the sharp brilliance of faceted gemstones, giving them a uniquely elegant and almost living appearance.

Jewelers, nobles, priests, artisans, and collectors prize pearls for their rarity, organic origin, gentle luster, and association with refinement and status. Fine pearls are commonly fashioned into necklaces, earrings, rings, bracelets, pendants, brooches, circlets, crowns, tiaras, hair ornaments, amulets, seals, and ceremonial garments, while larger or unusually shaped pearls may be preserved as treasures, religious offerings, royal decorations, or magical components. Perfectly spherical pearls with smooth surfaces, strong orient, large size, rare coloration, and exceptional luster are among the most desirable, though baroque pearls with unusual shapes resembling animals, faces, flowers, or symbols may also command great admiration. Pearls are frequently set in gold, silver, platinum, electrum, ivory, shell, coral, or carved wood and are especially suited to ornaments depicting moons, waves, seashells, swans, mermaids, dragons, stars, and other motifs associated with beauty, water, purity, and hidden treasures.

In many cultures, pearls are associated with purity, wisdom, prosperity, protection, transformation, and the mysteries of the sea. Sailors, merchants, rulers, priests, healers, nobles, aquatic peoples, elves, and adventurers sometimes carry pearls as symbols of fortune, divine favor, and treasures drawn from hidden depths. Their creation within living creatures may inspire legends that pearls are tears of sea spirits, hardened drops of moonlight, gifts from ocean deities, or fragments of wisdom formed over many years within sacred creatures. Coastal cultures may regard exceptional pearls as offerings worthy of kings and temples, while scholars and sages may compare their gradual formation to the accumulation of knowledge through patience and experience. Elven traditions may particularly prize flawless pearls for ceremonial jewelry representing harmony between land, sea, and sky. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though pearls are favored components for enchanted items concerned with water, healing, protection, wisdom, purification, communication, dreams, transformation, or the mysteries of the deep.

homebrew.name: Golden Fossilized Fern
homebrew.desc:
Golden Fossilized Fern

Golden fossilized fern is the preserved impression or mineralized remains of an ancient fern or fernlike plant distinguished by warm golden coloration produced by mineral replacement or staining. Trade and collector specimens are generally fist-sized or smaller and commonly consist of fragments bearing one or more clearly recognizable leaves or portions of a frond. The fossil itself ranges from pale yellow-gold and honey to ochre, bronze-gold, and rich metallic gold, often standing in striking contrast against gray, brown, black, cream, or tan matrix. Fine specimens preserve intricate stems and numerous individual leaflets, sometimes retaining remarkably delicate veins and branching patterns despite their immense age. Some examples possess a subtle metallic sheen where iron-bearing minerals or other deposits have replaced or coated the original plant material, while carefully prepared specimens may be lightly polished to enhance the contrast and golden appearance of the fossil.

Collectors, scholars, jewelers, and ornamental carvers value golden fossilized ferns for their delicate botanical patterns, unusual coloration, recognizable plant forms, and great antiquity. Small specimens with complete or nearly complete fronds may be preserved intact as curiosities, scholarly specimens, amulets, or decorative objects, while suitable fossil-bearing stone can be cut and polished into cabochons, pendants, brooches, seals, small plaques, and decorative inlays. Specimens displaying numerous intact leaflets, clearly visible veins, symmetrical branching, strong contrast with the surrounding matrix, pronounced golden mineralization, or an unusually complete small frond are particularly desirable. Golden fossilized ferns are frequently mounted in gold, bronze, brass, copper, electrum, or silver and are especially suited to ornaments depicting leaves, trees, branching vines, suns, and other motifs associated with nature, abundance, antiquity, and the passage of time.

In many cultures, golden fossilized ferns are associated with antiquity, memory, renewal, prosperity, enduring life, and the lost forests of the ancient world. Druids, herbalists, scholars, dwarven miners, natural philosophers, merchants, and explorers sometimes collect these fossils as tangible evidence of forests that flourished in ages long before recorded history. Druids may regard a delicate plant preserved in golden stone as a symbol that life can leave an enduring legacy long after its physical form has vanished, while dwarven traditions may interpret the combination of ancient vegetation and golden mineralization as an unusual union of the treasures of forest and earth. Some cultures regard particularly brilliant specimens as auspicious symbols of prosperity inherited from the distant past or of abundance returning after periods of hardship. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though golden fossilized ferns are favored components or decorations for enchanted items concerned with plants, earth, prosperity, knowledge, memory, regeneration, or creatures and environments of the distant past.
homebrew.unid:
Fossil

A fossil is the naturally preserved remains, impression, or trace of an ancient living creature or plant, found within stone or mineral deposits. For purposes of trade and collection, fossil specimens are generally fist-sized or smaller and may consist of shells, teeth, bones, leaves, wood, scales, small creatures, or recognizable impressions preserved within pieces of rock. Their colors vary widely according to the minerals that replaced or surrounded the original material and commonly include cream, tan, brown, gray, black, rust-red, and ochre. Particularly attractive specimens may contain contrasting mineral veins, crystalline cavities, or replacement minerals that accentuate the preserved structure. Some fossils are left in their natural matrix, while others are carefully cleaned, polished, or partially exposed to make their ancient forms easier to see.

Collectors, scholars, jewelers, and ornamental carvers value fossils according to their completeness, rarity, preservation, visual appeal, and the unusual nature of the creature or plant represented. Small shells, teeth, bones, leaves, and other recognizable specimens may be carried or displayed in small cases, while attractive fossil-bearing stones can be polished into cabochons, pendants, brooches, amulets, seals, beads, or decorative inlays. Especially desirable specimens include unusually complete fossils, exceptionally detailed impressions, rare creatures, attractive mineral replacement, or examples displaying structures such as teeth, scales, feathers, leaves, or delicate shell patterns with remarkable clarity. Fossils are frequently mounted in silver, bronze, copper, gold, or simple protective settings and are especially suited to ornaments depicting spirals, bones, shells, leaves, beasts, and other motifs associated with antiquity, nature, and the passage of time.

In many cultures, fossils are associated with antiquity, endurance, memory, ancestry, hidden knowledge, and the passage of time. Scholars, druids, dwarven miners, natural philosophers, and adventurers sometimes collect fossils as tangible evidence of creatures and landscapes that existed long before recorded history. Dwarven traditions may regard fossils uncovered deep within ancient stone as records preserved by the earth itself, while druids may view them as reminders that even the mightiest creatures eventually return to the land from which life arose. Scholars and explorers particularly prize unfamiliar fossils because they may provide clues concerning extinct creatures, vanished environments, or forgotten ages of the world. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though fossils are favored components or decorations for enchanted items concerned with earth, animals, plants, knowledge, memory, divination, or the creatures and events of the distant past.

homebrew.name: Golden Green Serpentine
homebrew.desc:
Golden Green Serpentine

Golden green serpentine is a rare and visually appealing variety of serpentine distinguished by its warm green coloration, golden-yellow highlights, smooth texture, and organic patterns reminiscent of sunlit forests and ancient landscapes. Serpentine is a group of hydrated magnesium silicate minerals that forms through the alteration of ultramafic rocks and commonly occurs alongside minerals such as magnetite, chromite, talc, and other serpentine varieties. Golden green serpentine ranges from pale yellow-green and olive to rich moss green, forest green, and deep green tones accented by golden, bronze, or honey-colored areas. Its coloration is caused by variations in mineral composition, iron compounds, and natural inclusions incorporated during formation. Fine specimens may display swirling patterns, mottled textures, veins, or layered areas that resemble leaves, roots, scales, or flowing streams beneath the polished surface. When expertly carved and polished, golden green serpentine develops a smooth waxy to silky luster and an appearance reminiscent of jade warmed by sunlight, ancient woodland stone, or living vegetation transformed into mineral.

Jewelers, sculptors, artisans, collectors, and ornamental carvers prize golden green serpentine for its unusual coloration, natural patterns, workability, and connection to the living world. Because serpentine is softer than many traditional gemstones, it is especially valued for carving and is commonly fashioned into figurines, bowls, plaques, seals, beads, amulets, boxes, gaming pieces, weapon fittings, ceremonial objects, and decorative panels. Fine material may also be cut into cabochons for rings, pendants, earrings, bracelets, and ornamental jewelry. Specimens possessing vivid green coloration, attractive golden highlights, intricate natural patterns, smooth polish, subtle translucence, substantial size, and minimal fractures are particularly desirable. Golden green serpentine is frequently mounted in gold, bronze, copper, electrum, silver, or carved wood settings and is especially suited to ornaments depicting trees, leaves, serpents, dragons, stags, suns, forests, and other motifs associated with nature, prosperity, renewal, and ancient earth wisdom.

In many cultures, golden green serpentine is associated with growth, prosperity, renewal, harmony, protection, and the balance between earth and sunlight. Druids, rangers, healers, elves, farmers, scholars, dwarven artisans, and adventurers sometimes carry golden green serpentine as a symbol of flourishing life, patient growth, and the hidden treasures of the natural world. Its combination of green and gold may inspire legends that it formed where sunlight touched sacred roots, where ancient forests met veins of precious earth, or where nature spirits blessed stones beneath the world's oldest trees. Elven traditions may value it as a representation of the harmony between forest and sun, while druids may associate it with cycles of growth, healing, and renewal. Merchants may regard its golden tones as a sign of abundance and good fortune, while scholars may study it as an example of nature's ability to blend strength and beauty. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though golden green serpentine is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with nature, healing, prosperity, protection, growth, fertility, transformation, communication with natural creatures, or the awakening of hidden life forces within the world.
homebrew.unid:
Serpentine

Serpentine is a distinctive and widely admired gemstone mineral group known for its rich green coloration, waxy luster, smooth texture, and association with the deep forces of the earth. It is a group of hydrated magnesium silicate minerals that commonly forms through the alteration of ultramafic rocks, often occurring alongside minerals such as magnetite, chromite, talc, and asbestos-forming serpentine varieties. Its colors range from pale yellow-green and olive to deep forest green, blackish green, brown-green, and mottled shades resembling leaves, moss, jade, or reptilian scales. Many specimens display intricate patterns, veins, clouding, or swirling variations caused by different mineral compositions and growth conditions. Fine material may possess a translucent quality along edges, while most gemstone-quality serpentine is opaque to semi-translucent. When expertly polished, serpentine develops a smooth waxy to greasy luster and an appearance reminiscent of polished jade, ancient forest stone, or living plant matter transformed into mineral form.

Jewelers, sculptors, artisans, collectors, and ornamental carvers prize serpentine for its attractive coloration, workability, durability, and natural patterns. Because it is softer than many traditional gemstones, serpentine is especially valued for carving rather than faceting and is commonly fashioned into figurines, bowls, plaques, seals, beads, amulets, decorative panels, boxes, gaming pieces, and ceremonial objects. Fine material may also be cut into cabochons for rings, pendants, earrings, bracelets, and ornamental jewelry. Specimens possessing vivid green coloration, attractive veining, smooth polish, unusual patterns, translucence, substantial size, and minimal fractures are particularly desirable. Serpentine is frequently mounted in silver, bronze, copper, gold, electrum, or natural wood settings and is especially suited to ornaments depicting serpents, dragons, trees, leaves, forests, mountains, spirits, and other motifs associated with earth, renewal, transformation, and ancient natural powers.

In many cultures, serpentine is associated with renewal, protection, transformation, wisdom, nature, and the hidden strength of the earth. Druids, healers, scholars, elves, dwarven artisans, priests, and adventurers sometimes carry serpentine as a symbol of growth, adaptation, and harmony with the natural world. Its resemblance to scales and flowing patterns may inspire legends that it formed from the shed skins of ancient world serpents, the bones of forest guardians, fragments of primordial earth spirits, or the hardened essence of creatures that guarded forgotten places. Nature traditions may value it as a stone of balance between living things and the earth, while dwarven cultures may associate it with the deep roots and hidden treasures of mountains. Scholars may regard its formation as evidence of the world's constant transformation, and adventurers may carry it as a token of resilience and safe passage through wild places. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though serpentine is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with nature, protection, transformation, healing, earth, poison resistance, ancient creatures, hidden places, communication with natural beings, or the enduring mysteries beneath the world's surface.

homebrew.name: Goldstone
homebrew.desc:
Goldstone

Goldstone is a glittering ornamental material distinguished by countless bright metallic-looking flecks suspended within a smooth, glassy body. Unlike naturally formed gemstones, goldstone is deliberately produced by skilled glassmakers who introduce copper or other metallic compounds into molten glass under carefully controlled conditions, allowing minute reflective crystals to form as the material cools. The traditional variety ranges from warm reddish brown and copper to deep rust and dark brown, densely filled with sparkling golden or copper-colored points. When turned beneath a light, these inclusions flash independently across the surface and interior, producing an appearance reminiscent of sparks, stars, or metallic dust suspended within polished stone. Properly cut and polished goldstone develops a bright glassy luster, with the finest material displaying an even distribution of brilliant reflective crystals throughout a richly colored and relatively uniform background.

Jewelers, glassmakers, and ornamental carvers prize goldstone for its intense sparkle, distinctive appearance, and the considerable craftsmanship required to produce consistently attractive material. It is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, pendants, earrings, brooches, bracelets, amulets, seals, gaming pieces, small figurines, decorative plaques, and ornamental inlays. Specimens displaying dense and evenly distributed metallic crystals, strong brilliance, rich background coloration, minimal bubbles or imperfections, and skillful cutting are particularly desirable. Large flawless pieces may also be carved into small vessels, statuettes, boxes, or ceremonial ornaments. Goldstone is frequently mounted in gold, bronze, brass, copper, electrum, or silver and is especially suited to ornaments depicting stars, suns, flames, constellations, dragons, and other motifs associated with light, fire, wealth, and celestial splendor.

In many cultures, goldstone is associated with ambition, prosperity, creativity, confidence, craftsmanship, and achievement through skill. Merchants, artisans, performers, nobles, astrologers, and adventurers sometimes wear goldstone as a symbol of success created through deliberate effort rather than discovered by chance. Because its glittering appearance is produced through skilled manufacture, guild traditions may regard especially fine goldstone as a celebration of mortal craftsmanship and the ability of artisans to transform ordinary materials into objects rivaling natural gems in beauty. Dwarven glassmakers and metalworkers may particularly appreciate the combination of fire, mineral ingredients, and technical precision required for its creation, while astrologers may associate its countless sparkling points with stars scattered across the heavens. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though goldstone is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with fire, light, prosperity, confidence, craftsmanship, luck, or celestial and divinatory themes.

homebrew.name: Gray Agate
homebrew.desc:
Gray Agate

Gray agate is a subdued and elegant variety of agate distinguished by its layered shades of silver-gray, charcoal, dove gray, smoky white, and muted stone tones. It is a microcrystalline form of quartz that develops through the gradual deposition of silica within cavities of volcanic rock, creating intricate internal layers and patterns over long periods of geological formation. Its characteristic bands may form sweeping curves, concentric rings, parallel lines, or irregular cloudlike patterns, sometimes interrupted by translucent areas that catch and diffuse the light. Fine specimens may reveal subtle variations between pale and dark gray layers, creating an appearance reminiscent of mist-covered mountains, ancient stone walls, storm clouds, or polished fragments of the earth's oldest foundations. When cut and polished, gray agate develops a smooth waxy-to-glassy luster that lends depth and refinement to its otherwise restrained coloration.

Jewelers, artisans, collectors, and ornamental carvers value gray agate for its understated elegance, durability, versatility, and ability to complement a wide variety of settings. It is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, rings, pendants, earrings, bracelets, signet stones, seals, cameos, gaming pieces, and small ornamental carvings. Specimens with sharply defined bands, unusual geometric formations, attractive cloudlike patterns, strong polish, and pleasing tonal contrast are particularly desirable. Gray agate pairs especially well with silver, platinum, iron, steel, bronze, and darker metals and is frequently incorporated into dwarven jewelry, military insignia, mourning pieces, ceremonial seals, ancestral heirlooms, and objects intended to convey dignity without ostentation. Its quiet appearance makes it well suited for ornaments emphasizing discipline, tradition, craftsmanship, and enduring strength.

In many cultures, gray agate is associated with stability, patience, wisdom, resolve, endurance, and calm judgment. Magistrates, soldiers, scholars, travelers, and leaders sometimes carry polished stones as symbols of sound reasoning, perseverance, and steadfastness during difficult circumstances. Dwarven traditions may regard the stone's layered gray bands as reflections of ancient mountain strata, connecting it with ancestry, deep earth, and the enduring strength of stone itself. Scholars may view its gradual formation as a reminder of patience and the accumulation of knowledge over time, while warriors may associate it with discipline and unwavering resolve. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though gray agate is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with endurance, mental fortitude, protection, resistance to earth and stone, ancestral memory, patience, or maintaining strength through hardship.

homebrew.name: Gray Angelite
homebrew.desc:
Gray Angelite

Gray angelite is a subdued and elegant variety of angelite distinguished by its cool shades of silver-gray, blue-gray, dove gray, and muted slate coloration. It is a variety of anhydrite, a calcium sulfate mineral formed in evaporite deposits and geological environments where gypsum has undergone natural dehydration over time. Its coloration ranges from soft misty gray and silvery tones to deeper slate and smoky blue-gray shades, often displaying cloudy white patches, pale blue undertones, or delicate veins that resemble drifting mist across an overcast sky. Fine specimens possess an even gray coloration with a subtle bluish cast, smooth texture, and few visible imperfections. When carefully polished, gray angelite develops a smooth, softly gleaming waxy luster rather than a brilliant sparkle, giving the stone a quiet, dignified appearance reminiscent of moonlit clouds, winter skies, or a fragment of the boundary between earth and heaven preserved within mineral form.

Jewelers, artisans, collectors, priests, and devotional craftsmen value gray angelite for its restrained elegance, unusual celestial character, and contemplative beauty. Because angelite is relatively soft and can be damaged by moisture, it requires careful cutting, handling, and protection from harsh conditions. It is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, rings, pendants, earrings, bracelets, brooches, amulets, devotional ornaments, seals, and small carved figures. Transparent material may be faceted for pendants, earrings, brooches, circlets, and ceremonial jewelry, while translucent or strongly banded specimens are commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, amulets, seals, figurines, decorative vessels, and ornamental carvings. Specimens possessing exceptional clarity, vivid coloration, pronounced multicolored zoning, or unusually large and perfectly formed crystals are especially desirable. Fluorite is frequently mounted in silver, gold, electrum, bronze, or platinum and is especially suited to ornaments depicting prisms, stars, eyes, geometric forms, and other motifs associated with knowledge, order, and mystical perception.

In many cultures, fluorite is associated with clarity, knowledge, order, concentration, transformation, and the perception of hidden patterns. Scholars, wizards, diviners, alchemists, and mathematicians sometimes keep polished stones or natural crystals as symbols of disciplined thought and the ability to discover order within seemingly chaotic information. Dwarven artisans may admire the mineral's precise geometric crystals as manifestations of the hidden structure of the earth, while arcane traditions sometimes interpret multicolored fluorite as a symbol of different magical forces brought into harmonious alignment. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though fluorite is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with mental clarity, knowledge, divination, concentration, detection of illusions, or the identification and analysis of magical effects.

homebrew.name: Hemetite
homebrew.desc:
Hematite

Hematite is a dense iron oxide mineral renowned for its metallic luster, substantial weight, and coloration ranging from steel gray and silvery black to dark reddish brown and nearly black. Metallic specimens may possess a brilliant reflective surface resembling polished iron or dark silver, while earthy varieties can appear dull red, brown, or ochre. Regardless of its outward appearance, hematite characteristically produces a reddish or reddish-brown streak when rubbed against an appropriate rough surface, revealing the iron-rich nature of the mineral. Natural specimens occur as compact masses, tabular crystals, rounded formations, and occasionally striking radiating or rosette-like structures. When carefully cut and polished, dense hematite develops an exceptionally smooth, highly reflective metallic surface that gives fashioned pieces the appearance of dark polished metal rather than ordinary stone.

Jewelers, metalworkers, collectors, and ornamental carvers prize hematite for its distinctive metallic appearance, durability, density, and ability to take a fine polish. Attractive material is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, pendants, earrings, brooches, bracelets, amulets, seals, signet stones, gaming pieces, small figurines, and decorative inlays. Naturally formed crystals, metallic rosettes, and other unusual specimens may be preserved intact as curiosities or incorporated directly into ornamental settings. Specimens possessing a brilliant metallic luster, smooth uniform surfaces, unusual crystal formations, substantial size, or particularly attractive natural textures are especially desirable. Hematite is frequently mounted in silver, iron, steel, bronze, copper, or darkened metal and is especially suited to ornaments depicting shields, swords, mountains, ravens, wolves, and other motifs associated with iron, warfare, strength, endurance, and the deep earth.

In many cultures, hematite is associated with strength, endurance, protection, courage, discipline, and connection to the earth. Warriors, miners, smiths, dwarven craftspeople, guards, and adventurers sometimes carry or wear polished hematite as a symbol of steadfastness and resilience in the face of danger. Its metallic appearance and iron-rich composition naturally encourage associations with weapons, armor, and the forge, while its hidden red streak may be interpreted as blood concealed beneath a surface of dark iron. Dwarven traditions may particularly esteem fine hematite as an embodiment of the strength and mineral wealth of the deep earth, while warrior cultures sometimes incorporate polished pieces into armor, weapon fittings, badges of rank, or memorial ornaments. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though hematite is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with earth, metal, protection, courage, endurance, physical resilience, or resistance to fear and hostile physical forces.

homebrew.name: Honey Calcite
homebrew.desc:
Honey Calcite

Honey calcite is a warm and luminous variety of calcite distinguished by rich shades of golden yellow, amber, honey, and caramel coloration. It is a carbonate mineral composed primarily of calcium carbonate, with its coloration typically produced by trace elements and mineral impurities within the crystal structure. Its hues may appear uniform or occur in cloudy layers, translucent bands, and irregular zones interspersed with cream, pale yellow, or warm brown areas. Fine specimens possess considerable translucency, allowing light to penetrate the stone and produce a soft golden glow reminiscent of sunlight passing through honey, polished amber, or a candle flame shining through warm glass. When carefully polished, honey calcite develops a smooth glassy-to-pearly luster that enhances its warmth, transparency, and internal depth.

Jewelers, ornamental carvers, collectors, artisans, and craftsmen value honey calcite for its inviting coloration, attractive patterns, and relative ease of carving. Because calcite is relatively soft and possesses perfect cleavage, it requires careful handling during cutting, polishing, and setting to prevent scratches, chips, and fractures. It is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, pendants, amulets, seals, figurines, decorative inlays, and small ornamental carvings, while especially attractive natural crystals are often preserved intact as collector's pieces, ceremonial objects, or geological curiosities. Specimens displaying rich golden coloration, strong translucency, unusual internal patterns, smooth polish, or attractive bands of honey and cream are particularly desirable. Honey calcite is frequently mounted in gold, bronze, copper, electrum, or other warm-toned metals and is especially suited to ornaments depicting suns, bees, wheat, coins, flames, harvest symbols, and other motifs associated with warmth, abundance, prosperity, and productive labor.

In many cultures, honey calcite is associated with prosperity, confidence, perseverance, productivity, abundance, success, and the rewards of patient labor. Merchants, craftspeople, farmers, miners, and builders sometimes carry polished stones as symbols of successful endeavors, steady progress, and wealth earned through diligence and skill. Its golden coloration may inspire legends that it formed from captured sunlight, the sweetness of ancient harvests preserved within the earth, or the hidden treasures of prosperous kingdoms long forgotten. Dwarven traditions may associate particularly rich golden specimens with valuable ores, the rewards of master craftsmanship, and the wealth concealed beneath the mountains. Agricultural communities may liken its warm hues to ripened grain, stored harvests, and the comfort of a well-stocked home. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though honey calcite is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with prosperity, confidence, endurance, craftsmanship, productivity, good fortune, or the discovery of hidden wealth.
homebrew.unid:
Calcite

Calcite is a common yet remarkably varied crystalline mineral prized for its extraordinary range of colors, distinctive crystal forms, and unusual interactions with light. It is a carbonate mineral composed primarily of calcium carbonate and occurs throughout the world in a vast array of geological environments. Pure calcite is colorless or white, but natural impurities and trace elements can produce shades of yellow, orange, red, pink, green, blue, brown, gray, and black. Transparent specimens are especially striking, as clear calcite can produce visible double images when viewed through certain crystal faces due to its strong optical properties. Natural crystals commonly form as angular rhombohedrons, pointed scalenohedrons, tabular forms, or intricate clustered formations, sometimes creating shapes resembling flowers, stars, or geometric sculptures. When carefully polished, calcite develops a smooth glassy-to-pearly luster that enhances its coloration, internal structure, and distinctive relationship with light.

Jewelers, ornamental carvers, collectors, scholars, and artisans value calcite for its variety, accessibility, unusual optical properties, and ease of working. Because calcite is relatively soft and possesses perfect cleavage, it is vulnerable to scratches, chips, and breakage and requires careful handling when used in decorative pieces. Attractive material is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, pendants, amulets, decorative inlays, figurines, vessels, seals, and larger ornamental carvings, while exceptional transparent crystals or well-formed natural specimens are often preserved intact as collector's pieces, scholarly curiosities, or ceremonial objects. Specimens possessing unusual coloration, exceptional clarity, strong banding, dramatic internal structures, or impressive crystal formations are particularly desirable. Calcite is frequently mounted in silver, bronze, copper, gold, electrum, or other metals and is especially suited to ornaments depicting prisms, mountains, eyes, geometric forms, crystals, and other motifs associated with earth, structure, perception, and hidden patterns.

In many cultures, calcite is associated with clarity, stability, transformation, insight, perception, and the hidden order of the earth. Miners, masons, scholars, philosophers, and elemental practitioners sometimes regard its varied crystalline forms as demonstrations of the intricate structures concealed within ordinary stone. Its ability to split light and reveal double images may inspire legends that clear calcite allows mortals to perceive truths hidden behind appearances, recognize multiple possibilities, or understand realities that others overlook. Particularly transparent specimens may be associated with honesty, revelation, and the separation of illusion from reality, while dwarven traditions may prize large, perfectly formed crystals as symbols of precision, patience, and masterful stonework. Elemental scholars may view calcite as evidence of the earth's ability to transform simple materials into complex and beautiful structures over vast periods of time. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though calcite is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with earth, perception, transformation, mental clarity, optical effects, the detection of illusions, or the revelation of hidden things.

homebrew.name: Iridescent Fossilized Fern
homebrew.desc:
Iridescent Fossilized Fern

Iridescent fossilized fern is the preserved impression or mineralized remains of an ancient fern or fernlike plant distinguished by mineral deposits that produce shifting flashes of color across portions of the fossil. Trade and collector specimens are generally fist-sized or smaller and commonly consist of fragments bearing one or more clearly recognizable leaves or portions of a frond. The underlying fossil may be gray, brown, black, bronze, or silvery, while thin layers of mineralization produce iridescent flashes of blue, green, violet, gold, copper, and occasionally reddish hues when the specimen is turned beneath the light. Fine specimens preserve intricate stems and numerous individual leaflets, sometimes retaining delicate veins and branching patterns beneath the colorful mineral sheen. Particularly striking examples combine a clearly recognizable botanical form with strong, naturally occurring iridescence that changes noticeably according to the angle of illumination.

Collectors, scholars, jewelers, and ornamental carvers value iridescent fossilized ferns for their delicate botanical patterns, unusual optical appearance, great antiquity, and rarity. Small specimens with complete or nearly complete fronds may be preserved intact as curiosities, scholarly specimens, amulets, or decorative objects, while suitable fossil-bearing stone can be carefully cut and polished into cabochons, pendants, brooches, seals, small plaques, and decorative inlays. Specimens displaying numerous intact leaflets, clearly visible veins, symmetrical branching, strong natural iridescence, numerous shifting colors, or an unusually complete small frond are particularly desirable. Iridescent fossilized ferns are frequently mounted in silver, electrum, gold, bronze, or darkened metal and are especially suited to ornaments depicting leaves, trees, rainbows, stars, branching vines, and other motifs associated with nature, transformation, antiquity, and the passage of time.

In many cultures, iridescent fossilized ferns are associated with antiquity, transformation, memory, renewal, hidden beauty, and the persistence of life through time. Druids, herbalists, scholars, dwarven miners, natural philosophers, diviners, and explorers sometimes collect these fossils as remarkable examples of ancient life transformed by the earth into something possessing an entirely new form of beauty. Druids may regard the shifting colors of a plant preserved in stone as a symbol that death and transformation are parts of nature's continuing cycles, while dwarven scholars may interpret the iridescent mineralization as evidence that the earth can embellish and preserve the records entrusted to it. Some divinatory traditions regard the changing colors as symbolic of the many different truths that can be discovered by examining the past from different perspectives. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though iridescent fossilized ferns are favored components or decorations for enchanted items concerned with plants, earth, transformation, knowledge, memory, divination, illusions, or creatures and environments of the distant past.
homebrew.unid:
Fossil

A fossil is the naturally preserved remains, impression, or trace of an ancient living creature or plant, found within stone or mineral deposits. For purposes of trade and collection, fossil specimens are generally fist-sized or smaller and may consist of shells, teeth, bones, leaves, wood, scales, small creatures, or recognizable impressions preserved within pieces of rock. Their colors vary widely according to the minerals that replaced or surrounded the original material and commonly include cream, tan, brown, gray, black, rust-red, and ochre. Particularly attractive specimens may contain contrasting mineral veins, crystalline cavities, or replacement minerals that accentuate the preserved structure. Some fossils are left in their natural matrix, while others are carefully cleaned, polished, or partially exposed to make their ancient forms easier to see.

Collectors, scholars, jewelers, and ornamental carvers value fossils according to their completeness, rarity, preservation, visual appeal, and the unusual nature of the creature or plant represented. Small shells, teeth, bones, leaves, and other recognizable specimens may be carried or displayed in small cases, while attractive fossil-bearing stones can be polished into cabochons, pendants, brooches, amulets, seals, beads, or decorative inlays. Especially desirable specimens include unusually complete fossils, exceptionally detailed impressions, rare creatures, attractive mineral replacement, or examples displaying structures such as teeth, scales, feathers, leaves, or delicate shell patterns with remarkable clarity. Fossils are frequently mounted in silver, bronze, copper, gold, or simple protective settings and are especially suited to ornaments depicting spirals, bones, shells, leaves, beasts, and other motifs associated with antiquity, nature, and the passage of time.

In many cultures, fossils are associated with antiquity, endurance, memory, ancestry, hidden knowledge, and the passage of time. Scholars, druids, dwarven miners, natural philosophers, and adventurers sometimes collect fossils as tangible evidence of creatures and landscapes that existed long before recorded history. Dwarven traditions may regard fossils uncovered deep within ancient stone as records preserved by the earth itself, while druids may view them as reminders that even the mightiest creatures eventually return to the land from which life arose. Scholars and explorers particularly prize unfamiliar fossils because they may provide clues concerning extinct creatures, vanished environments, or forgotten ages of the world. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though fossils are favored components or decorations for enchanted items concerned with earth, animals, plants, knowledge, memory, divination, or the creatures and events of the distant past.

homebrew.name: Lapis Lazuli
homebrew.desc:
Lapis Lazuli

Lapis lazuli is a richly colored ornamental stone renowned for its intense blue coloration and frequent inclusions of golden pyrite and white calcite. Rather than a single mineral, lapis lazuli is a rock composed primarily of blue lazurite together with varying amounts of calcite, pyrite, sodalite, and other minerals. Its hues range from medium royal blue and ultramarine to deep azure and intense midnight blue, with the finest material displaying strong, evenly distributed blue coloration. Tiny crystals of metallic pyrite often appear as scattered golden specks or delicate veins, giving polished specimens the appearance of stars scattered across a deep blue sky. White or pale gray calcite may occur as streaks, clouds, or patches; small amounts can create attractive contrast, while extensive pale material generally reduces the value of gem-quality specimens. Lapis lazuli is opaque and develops a smooth waxy to glassy luster when carefully cut and polished.

Jewelers, sculptors, painters, and ornamental carvers prize lapis lazuli for its magnificent blue coloration, distinctive golden inclusions, ability to take a fine polish, and suitability for intricate decorative work. Fine material is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, pendants, earrings, bracelets, brooches, rings, amulets, seals, signet stones, gaming pieces, and decorative inlays, while larger pieces may be carved into figurines, plaques, boxes, small vessels, religious objects, weapon fittings, and ceremonial ornaments. Particularly fine lapis may also be ground into a brilliant blue pigment for illuminated manuscripts, paintings, murals, and other prestigious works of art, making high-quality material valuable to artists as well as jewelers. Specimens possessing intense ultramarine or royal-blue coloration, evenly scattered golden pyrite, minimal intrusive calcite, fine texture, substantial size, or unusually attractive natural patterns are particularly desirable. Lapis lazuli is frequently mounted in gold, electrum, silver, bronze, or copper and is especially suited to ornaments depicting stars, eyes, suns, moons, crowns, birds, and other motifs associated with the heavens, wisdom, royalty, and divine authority.

In many cultures, lapis lazuli is associated with wisdom, truth, nobility, divine favor, knowledge, and the heavens. Rulers, priests, scholars, astrologers, scribes, judges, diplomats, and wealthy adventurers sometimes wear lapis lazuli as a symbol of cultivated knowledge and authority guided by wisdom rather than force alone. Its deep blue coloration flecked with golden pyrite naturally invites comparison to a star-filled night sky, encouraging celestial traditions to incorporate it into objects associated with astronomy, prophecy, deities of the heavens, and royal legitimacy. Scholars and scribes may especially prize lapis because the finest material can provide both gemstones and prestigious blue pigment, while royal courts may incorporate exceptional specimens into crowns, seals, scepters, ceremonial weapons, and sacred regalia. Dwarven artisans may admire the golden mineral inclusions within the blue stone as miniature veins of metal preserved naturally within rock, while elven craftsmen may favor star-speckled specimens for celestial ornaments. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though lapis lazuli is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with knowledge, truth, divination, mental clarity, celestial phenomena, authority, or protection against deception and illusions.

homebrew.name: Light Green Malachite
homebrew.desc:
Light Green Malachite

Light green malachite is an attractive form of malachite distinguished by softer green coloration and the characteristic natural banding produced during the mineral's growth. Its hues range from pale grass green and fresh leaf green to soft mint, celadon, and medium green, commonly accompanied by bands, rings, veins, or patches of darker emerald, forest, or bluish green. Particularly fine specimens display sharply defined layers arranged in concentric eyes, sweeping curves, irregular stripes, or elaborate swirling patterns. Natural malachite may occur as compact masses, rounded nodules, crusts, stalactitic formations, or delicate radiating and fibrous growths. Although generally opaque, finely polished material can possess considerable visual depth, with lighter areas making subtle variations in banding especially easy to see. When expertly cut and polished, light green malachite develops a smooth glassy to silky luster that enriches its gentle coloration and reveals intricate patterns that may be difficult to appreciate in the rough stone.

Jewelers, sculptors, and ornamental carvers prize light green malachite for its graceful coloration, distinctive natural patterns, ability to take a fine polish, and suitability for both jewelry and decorative objects. Attractive material is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, pendants, earrings, bracelets, brooches, rings, amulets, seals, gaming pieces, and decorative inlays, while larger masses may be carved into figurines, plaques, boxes, bowls, small vessels, weapon fittings, and elaborate ornamental objects. Skilled artisans carefully orient each cut to emphasize concentric eyes, sweeping bands, symmetrical markings, or attractive transitions between pale and deeper green. Specimens possessing clear light green coloration, sharply defined darker banding, numerous concentric eyes, substantial size, minimal fractures, or unusually intricate natural patterns are particularly desirable. Light green malachite is frequently mounted in silver, gold, bronze, copper, electrum, or carved wooden settings and is especially suited to ornaments depicting leaves, vines, flowers, eyes, serpents, butterflies, and other motifs associated with nature, growth, prosperity, and renewal.

In many cultures, light green malachite is associated with renewal, vitality, prosperity, protection, growth, and the fertile power of the earth. Druids, healers, farmers, merchants, miners, elven artisans, dwarven craftsmen, and adventurers sometimes carry light green malachite as a symbol of new growth and prosperity gradually emerging from the earth. Its softer coloration may cause woodland and agricultural cultures to compare it to young leaves, spring vegetation, and newly planted fields, making it particularly appropriate for traditions concerned with beginnings, fertility, and recovery after hardship. Elven artisans may favor specimens whose bands resemble leaves, vines, or flowing water, while dwarven craftsmen may prize the visible patterns as evidence of copper-bearing minerals formed within the stone. The concentric eye-like markings found in some specimens may also encourage their use as symbols of vigilance and protection against unseen dangers. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though light green malachite is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with earth, plants, renewal, protection, prosperity, healing, metal, or the detection of poison and hidden dangers.

Skilled artisans carefully orient each cut to reveal concentric eyes, sweeping bands, symmetrical patterns, or unusual natural designs, and exceptional pieces may be assembled so their banding forms mirrored or continuous patterns across a larger surface. homebrew.name: Light Turquoise
homebrew.desc:
Light Turquoise

Light turquoise is a delicate and highly admired variety of turquoise distinguished by its pale blue coloration, soft appearance, and association with clear skies, peaceful waters, and gentle protection. Turquoise is a hydrated phosphate mineral composed primarily of copper and aluminum, forming in arid regions where copper-rich groundwater interacts with aluminum and phosphorus-bearing minerals. Light turquoise ranges in color from pale sky blue and robin's egg blue to soft aqua, powder blue, and faint blue-green shades, with coloration influenced primarily by copper content and variations in mineral composition. Fine specimens may display a smooth even color, subtle cloudy patterns, or delicate matrix markings of brown, gray, or black that resemble wisps of clouds, distant mountains, or flowing streams. When polished, light turquoise develops a smooth waxy to subvitreous luster and an appearance reminiscent of morning skies, calm ocean waters, frost-touched stone, or fragments of peaceful celestial realms captured within mineral form.

Jewelers, artisans, nobles, collectors, and master craftsmen prize light turquoise for its graceful coloration, traditional significance, soothing appearance, and versatility in decorative work. Fine material is commonly fashioned into cabochons for rings, pendants, earrings, bracelets, necklaces, brooches, amulets, seals, beads, ceremonial objects, and elegant jewelry, while larger specimens may be carved into figurines, plaques, boxes, inlays, gaming pieces, and ornamental treasures. Specimens possessing clear pale blue coloration, smooth texture, attractive natural patterns, strong polish, solid structure, substantial size, and minimal fractures are particularly desirable. Light turquoise is frequently mounted in silver, white gold, platinum, copper, bronze, electrum, or pale natural materials and is especially suited to ornaments depicting clouds, birds, feathers, waves, stars, moons, flowers, temples, and other motifs associated with peace, protection, travel, purity, and harmony with the natural world.

In many cultures, light turquoise is associated with peace, healing, communication, protection, hope, and the gentle guidance of sky and water. Travelers, healers, diplomats, priests, sailors, scholars, wizards, and adventurers sometimes carry light turquoise as a symbol of safe journeys, friendship, and calm understanding. Its pale coloration may inspire legends that it formed from the first drops of sacred rain, pieces of the morning sky that descended to earth, the breath of benevolent spirits, or waters blessed by celestial guardians. Sailors may regard it as a token of favorable winds and peaceful seas, while diplomats may associate it with honest communication and reconciliation. Healers may value it as a symbol of restoration and emotional balance, while scholars may see it as a reminder of knowledge carried across generations like rivers flowing through the world. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though light turquoise is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with protection, healing, communication, travel, diplomacy, weather, water, dreams, purification, or creating harmony between individuals and the world around them.
homebrew.unid:
Turquoise

Turquoise is one of the most ancient and revered ornamental gemstones, prized for its distinctive blue-green coloration, opaque beauty, and long association with protection, wisdom, and sacred traditions. It is a hydrated phosphate mineral composed primarily of copper and aluminum, forming in arid regions where copper-rich groundwater interacts with aluminum and phosphorus-bearing minerals. Turquoise ranges in color from pale sky blue and robin's egg blue to vivid turquoise, green-blue, teal, and green shades, with coloration primarily influenced by copper and iron content. homebrew.name: Malacite
homebrew.desc:
Malachite

Malachite is a distinctive copper carbonate mineral renowned for its vivid green coloration and dramatic natural banding. Its hues range from pale mint and bright grass green to rich emerald, deep forest green, and nearly black-green, commonly occurring together in concentric bands, sweeping curves, irregular stripes, and rounded patterns. Particularly fine specimens display alternating layers of light and dark green that form eyes, rings, waves, or complex swirling designs when cut across the mineral's growth structure. Natural malachite may occur as compact masses, crusts, rounded nodules, stalactitic formations, or delicate radiating and fibrous crystals. Although generally opaque, finely polished material possesses remarkable visual depth, with contrasting bands creating the illusion of folds, ripples, or layered landscapes beneath the surface. When expertly cut and polished, malachite develops a smooth glassy to silky luster that intensifies its green coloration and reveals patterns often concealed within the rough stone.

Jewelers, sculptors, and ornamental carvers prize malachite for its extraordinary patterns, intense coloration, ability to take a fine polish, and suitability for both jewelry and larger decorative objects. Skilled artisans carefully orient each cut to reveal concentric eyes, sweeping bands, symmetrical patterns, or unusual natural designs, and exceptional pieces may be assembled so their banding forms mirrored or continuous patterns across a larger surface. Specimens possessing vivid green coloration, sharply contrasting bands, numerous concentric eyes, unusual natural formations, substantial size, or particularly intricate patterns are especially desirable. Malachite is frequently mounted in gold, silver, bronze, copper, electrum, or darkened metal and is especially suited to ornaments depicting eyes, serpents, dragons, leaves, vines, peacock feathers, and other motifs associated with nature, wealth, transformation, and the earth.

In many cultures, malachite is associated with prosperity, protection, transformation, vitality, abundance, and the hidden wealth of the earth. Dwarven craftsmen may particularly prize intricately banded specimens as natural works of subterranean art, while druids and woodland peoples may associate their intense greens with vigorous plant life and continual renewal. homebrew.name: Merlinite

Merlinite is frequently mounted in silver, platinum, electrum, white gold, iron, or darkened metal and is especially suited to ornaments depicting trees, ravens, moons, mountains, mist, towers, and other motifs associated with mystery, wilderness, knowledge, and transformation.

Mottled Brown Petrified Wood

Mottled brown petrified wood is the fossilized remains of ancient wood in which the original organic material has been gradually replaced by minerals while retaining much of the wood's original structure. Trade and collector specimens are generally fist-sized or smaller and display irregular mixtures of tan, ochre, caramel, chestnut, reddish brown, chocolate, and dark earthy brown. These colors may occur as patches, streaks, bands, or concentric areas following the original grain and growth patterns of the wood, producing a richly variegated appearance. Fine specimens preserve recognizable growth rings, grain, bark textures, knots, or cellular structures that clearly reveal their origin despite their transformation into stone. Broken surfaces may be rough and stonelike, while carefully cut and polished specimens develop a smooth glassy-to-waxy luster that accentuates the mottled coloration and intricate preserved grain.

Collectors, scholars, jewelers, and ornamental carvers value mottled brown petrified wood for its varied earthy colors, recognizable organic structure, mineral durability, and individuality, since no two pieces possess precisely the same pattern. Small natural fragments may be preserved intact as curiosities, amulets, or scholarly specimens, while attractive material can be cut and polished into cabochons, beads, pendants, brooches, seals, small plaques, figurines, and decorative inlays. Specimens displaying sharply defined growth rings, intricate grain patterns, preserved bark, numerous contrasting shades of brown, unusual mineral veins, or particularly attractive mottling are especially desirable. Mottled brown petrified wood is frequently mounted in bronze, copper, brass, gold, silver, or iron and is especially suited to ornaments depicting trees, roots, leaves, mountains, animals, and other motifs associated with nature, antiquity, endurance, and the earth.

In many cultures, mottled brown petrified wood is associated with antiquity, endurance, memory, transformation, stability, and the enduring cycles of nature. Druids, dwarven miners, scholars, rangers, natural philosophers, and travelers sometimes carry small polished specimens as symbols of strength gained through gradual change and the enduring connection between living things and the earth. Druids may regard the preserved grain and varied earthy colors as a record of a tree's passage from living forest to enduring stone, while dwarven traditions sometimes interpret petrified wood as evidence that the earth can preserve and strengthen what time would otherwise destroy. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though mottled brown petrified wood is a favored component or decoration for enchanted items concerned with plants, earth, endurance, transformation, memory, protection, or the environments and events of the distant past.

For purposes of trade and collection, fossil specimens are generally fist-sized or smaller and may consist of shells, teeth, bones, leaves, wood, scales, small creatures, or recognizable impressions preserved within pieces of rock. homebrew.name: Obsidian
homebrew.desc:
Obsidian

Obsidian is a naturally occurring volcanic glass formed when silica-rich molten rock cools so rapidly that crystals have little or no opportunity to develop. Although best known for its deep black coloration, obsidian may also occur in dark brown, smoky gray, reddish brown, greenish black, or combinations of these colors, sometimes displaying bands, spots, metallic sheens, or other distinctive optical effects. Freshly broken obsidian possesses an exceptionally smooth, glassy surface and typically fractures in curved, shell-like patterns known as conchoidal fractures. These fractures can produce edges of extraordinary sharpness, allowing carefully worked obsidian to form cutting surfaces finer than those achievable with many ordinary metals. Transparent or translucent areas may become visible along thin edges when held before a strong light, even when a larger specimen appears completely opaque. When expertly polished, obsidian develops a brilliant glassy luster and a dark reflective surface resembling polished black glass.

Jewelers, weaponsmiths, sculptors, and ornamental carvers prize obsidian for its intense coloration, brilliant polish, exceptional sharpness when fractured, and suitability for both decorative and practical objects. Fine material is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, pendants, earrings, bracelets, brooches, rings, amulets, seals, gaming pieces, mirrors, and decorative inlays, while larger pieces may be carved into figurines, masks, plaques, bowls, ritual objects, and polished spheres. Skilled flintknappers can fracture obsidian into razor-edged knives, spearheads, arrowheads, surgical blades, and cutting tools, though such edges are brittle and can chip or shatter under heavy impact. Large flawless pieces suitable for mirrors, elaborate carvings, or long blades are particularly desirable, as are specimens possessing unusual coloration, distinctive inclusions, strong optical effects, or exceptionally uniform texture. Obsidian is frequently mounted in silver, gold, electrum, bronze, copper, iron, or darkened steel and is especially suited to ornaments depicting ravens, dragons, flames, eyes, skulls, mountains, and other motifs associated with darkness, fire, vigilance, and hidden power.

In many cultures, obsidian is associated with protection, truth, fire, darkness, transformation, vigilance, and the dangerous power beneath the earth. Priests, warriors, diviners, assassins, volcanic peoples, dwarven artisans, wizards, and adventurers sometimes carry obsidian as a symbol of destructive forces transformed into something beautiful and useful. Its origin in molten rock may cause cultures living near volcanoes to regard it as frozen fire, the blood or tears of mountain deities, or remnants of subterranean furnaces brought to the surface. Polished black obsidian mirrors may be associated with divination, visions, spirits, and the revelation of concealed truths, while its extraordinarily sharp edges encourage associations with sacrifice, warfare, precision, and decisive action. Dwarven craftsmen may admire obsidian as stone transformed into glass by natural heat, while priests of fire or earth deities may incorporate it into ceremonial weapons and sacred objects. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though obsidian is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with fire, earth, protection, divination, darkness, truth, cutting, or the detection of hidden and invisible things.

homebrew.name: Pyrite Nugget

Stream-worn specimens may develop smoother surfaces, while pieces recovered directly from mineral veins commonly retain angular crystals, attached quartz, or fragments of surrounding rock. homebrew.name: Rainbow Obsidian
homebrew.desc:
Rainbow Obsidian

Rainbow obsidian is a striking variety of volcanic glass distinguished by subtle bands of iridescent color that emerge from an otherwise black or very dark surface when viewed beneath strong light. Like other obsidian, it forms when silica-rich molten rock cools so rapidly that crystals have little or no opportunity to develop. Its underlying body color is typically deep black, charcoal, or smoky black-brown, while microscopic mineral inclusions and internal structures produce shimmering bands or concentric layers of green, violet, blue, gold, bronze, red, pink, and occasionally several colors together. These colors are often subdued when the stone is viewed casually but become dramatically visible when a polished surface is tilted toward the light. Particularly fine specimens display several distinct bands arranged in concentric arcs, flowing curves, or overlapping rings. When expertly cut and polished, rainbow obsidian develops a brilliant glassy luster and a remarkable depth in which colored reflections seem to hover within an otherwise dark stone.

Jewelers, sculptors, and ornamental carvers prize rainbow obsidian for its multicolored iridescence, deep black body color, brilliant polish, and dramatic transformation under changing illumination. Fine material is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, pendants, earrings, bracelets, brooches, rings, amulets, seals, gaming pieces, polished spheres, and decorative inlays, while larger pieces may be carved into figurines, masks, plaques, bowls, mirrors, boxes, and ceremonial objects. Skilled artisans carefully orient each cut to intersect the internal layers at angles that reveal the strongest colors, sometimes producing concentric rainbow patterns across broad polished surfaces. Specimens possessing numerous distinct colors, intense iridescence, symmetrical bands or rings, substantial size, minimal fractures, or particularly vivid red, violet, blue, and green reflections are especially desirable. Rainbow obsidian is frequently mounted in silver, gold, platinum, electrum, bronze, copper, or darkened metal and is especially suited to ornaments depicting eyes, peacock feathers, dragons, ravens, butterflies, auroras, eclipses, and other motifs associated with transformation, hidden beauty, darkness, and supernatural light.

In many cultures, rainbow obsidian is associated with transformation, revelation, hidden potential, protection, mystery, and hope emerging from darkness. Diviners, priests, artists, volcanic peoples, elven artisans, dwarven craftsmen, wizards, and adventurers sometimes carry rainbow obsidian as a symbol of extraordinary possibilities concealed beneath an unassuming exterior. Its brilliant colors appearing only when an apparently black stone is viewed from the proper direction may inspire legends that rainbows, auroras, or fragments of celestial fire became trapped within volcanic glass as it cooled. Dwarven traditions may interpret the hidden colors as remnants of the subterranean fires that created the stone, while elven artisans may prize specimens whose shifting bands resemble auroras or magical light against a night sky. Diviners and philosophers may regard the appearance of color within darkness as a reminder that truths, opportunities, and beauty can remain concealed until circumstances allow them to be seen. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though rainbow obsidian is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with fire, protection, illusions, divination, transformation, light, darkness, or the detection of hidden and invisible things.
homebrew.unid:
Obsidian

Freshly broken obsidian possesses an exceptionally smooth, glassy surface and typically fractures in curved, shell-like patterns known as conchoidal fractures. These fractures can produce edges of extraordinary sharpness, allowing carefully worked obsidian to form cutting surfaces finer than those achievable with many ordinary metals. Transparent or translucent areas may become visible along thin edges when held before a strong light, even when a larger specimen appears completely opaque. When expertly polished, obsidian develops a brilliant glassy luster and a dark reflective surface resembling polished black glass.

Jewelers, weaponsmiths, sculptors, and ornamental carvers prize obsidian for its intense coloration, brilliant polish, exceptional sharpness when fractured, and suitability for both decorative and practical objects. Fine material is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, pendants, earrings, bracelets, brooches, rings, amulets, seals, gaming pieces, mirrors, and decorative inlays, while larger pieces may be carved into figurines, masks, plaques, bowls, ritual objects, and polished spheres. Skilled flintknappers can fracture obsidian into razor-edged knives, spearheads, arrowheads, surgical blades, and cutting tools, though such edges are brittle and can chip or shatter under heavy impact. Large flawless pieces suitable for mirrors, elaborate carvings, or long blades are particularly desirable, as are specimens possessing unusual coloration, distinctive inclusions, strong optical effects, or exceptionally uniform texture. Obsidian is frequently mounted in silver, gold, electrum, bronze, copper, iron, or darkened steel and is especially suited to ornaments depicting ravens, dragons, flames, eyes, skulls, mountains, and other motifs associated with darkness, fire, vigilance, and hidden power.

In many cultures, obsidian is associated with protection, truth, fire, darkness, transformation, vigilance, and the dangerous power beneath the earth. Priests, warriors, diviners, assassins, volcanic peoples, dwarven artisans, wizards, and adventurers sometimes carry obsidian as a symbol of destructive forces transformed into something beautiful and useful. Polished black obsidian mirrors may be associated with divination, visions, spirits, and the revelation of concealed truths, while its extraordinarily sharp edges encourage associations with sacrifice, warfare, precision, and decisive action. Dwarven craftsmen may admire obsidian as stone transformed into glass by natural heat, while priests of fire or earth deities may incorporate it into ceremonial weapons and sacred objects. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though obsidian is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with fire, earth, protection, divination, darkness, truth, cutting, or the detection of hidden and invisible things.

homebrew.name: Red Agate
homebrew.desc:
Red Agate

Red agate is a richly colored and highly admired variety of agate distinguished by its warm shades of crimson, brick red, rust, scarlet, and reddish-brown coloration. It is a microcrystalline form of quartz that develops through the gradual deposition of silica within cavities of volcanic rock, creating layered structures and intricate patterns over long periods of geological formation. Its colors are influenced primarily by iron compounds and other mineral impurities, producing the gemstone's characteristic warm and earthy tones. Red agate may display fine parallel lines, sweeping curves, concentric rings, irregular patches, or contrasting layers of cream, white, gray, and deeper scarlet. Fine specimens may possess translucent areas that reveal a warm inner glow when held before strong light, creating an appearance reminiscent of glowing embers, ancient banners, fired clay, or the heart of a forge preserved within stone. When cut and polished, red agate develops a smooth waxy-to-glassy luster that enhances its bold coloration and natural patterns.

Jewelers, artisans, collectors, and ornamental carvers value red agate for its rich coloration, durability, versatility, and ability to take an excellent polish. It is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, rings, pendants, earrings, bracelets, signet stones, seals, amulets, gaming pieces, and small ornamental carvings. Specimens possessing deep evenly saturated red tones, sharply contrasting bands, attractive natural patterns, smooth polish, and pleasing translucence are particularly desirable among collectors and craftsmen. Red agate is frequently mounted in gold, bronze, copper, electrum, or darkened steel, with warm metals enhancing its fiery appearance. It is especially popular in martial jewelry, heraldic ornaments, ceremonial seals, clan heirlooms, and decorative pieces depicting lions, dragons, flames, swords, shields, and other symbols of strength, courage, and enduring power.

In many cultures, red agate is associated with strength, courage, vitality, loyalty, protection, and the enduring will to overcome adversity. Warriors, guards, champions, travelers, and leaders sometimes carry polished stones as talismans of steadfastness, resilience, and protection against injury or misfortune. Its deep red coloration may inspire legends that it formed from ancient battlefields, the blood of legendary heroes, the fires of sacred forges, or the iron-rich foundations of the world itself. Dwarven traditions may associate the stone's coloration with blood, iron, and the heat of the forge, making it a symbol of physical endurance, craftsmanship, loyalty to clan, and the strength required to endure hardship. Soldiers may regard it as a token of bravery, while artisans may value it as a reminder of dedication and mastery. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though red agate is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with courage, physical resilience, protection, martial prowess, endurance, loyalty, or strengthening the resolve of its bearer.

homebrew.name: Red Aventurine
homebrew.desc:
Red Aventurine

It is a variety of quartz containing countless tiny mineral inclusions that create its characteristic glittering effect, known as aventurescence. These reflective inclusions are scattered throughout the stone and produce flashes of copper, gold, red, or silver as the gemstone is turned in the light. The finest specimens possess rich, even red coloration combined with abundant, finely distributed sparkle, creating an appearance reminiscent of glowing embers, polished copper warmed by firelight, or sparks rising from a forge. When polished, red aventurine develops a smooth glassy luster that enhances both its bold coloration and distinctive natural shimmer.

Jewelers, ornamental carvers, collectors, artisans, and warriors value red aventurine for its striking coloration, durability, natural sparkle, and powerful visual character. It is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, rings, pendants, earrings, bracelets, brooches, amulets, seals, decorative inlays, and small ornamental carvings. Specimens possessing deep red coloration, strong aventurescence, evenly distributed reflective inclusions, smooth polish, and attractive patterns are particularly desirable. Red aventurine is frequently mounted in gold, copper, bronze, electrum, or darkened silver and is especially suited to jewelry depicting flames, lions, dragons, weapons, shields, coins, crowns, and other motifs associated with courage, strength, victory, determination, and favorable fortune.

In many cultures, red aventurine is associated with courage, vitality, determination, luck, decisive action, and success through bold choices. homebrew.name: Red Fossilized Fern
homebrew.desc:
Red Fossilized Fern

Red fossilized fern is the preserved impression or mineralized remains of an ancient fern or fernlike plant distinguished by red coloration produced by mineral replacement or staining. Trade and collector specimens are generally fist-sized or smaller and commonly consist of fragments bearing one or more clearly recognizable leaves or portions of a frond. The fossil itself ranges from muted brick red and rust to terracotta, reddish brown, crimson, and deep iron-red, often standing in striking contrast against cream, tan, gray, brown, or black matrix. Fine specimens preserve intricate stems and numerous individual leaflets, sometimes retaining remarkably delicate veins and branching patterns despite their immense age. Some examples display variations of red and orange caused by iron-rich minerals, while carefully prepared specimens may be lightly polished to enhance the contrast and rich coloration of the fossil.

Collectors, scholars, jewelers, and ornamental carvers value red fossilized ferns for their delicate botanical patterns, distinctive coloration, recognizable plant forms, and great antiquity. Small specimens with complete or nearly complete fronds may be preserved intact as curiosities, scholarly specimens, amulets, or decorative objects, while suitable fossil-bearing stone can be cut and polished into cabochons, pendants, brooches, seals, small plaques, and decorative inlays. Specimens displaying numerous intact leaflets, clearly visible veins, symmetrical branching, strong contrast with the surrounding matrix, rich red mineralization, or an unusually complete small frond are particularly desirable. Red fossilized ferns are frequently mounted in bronze, copper, gold, electrum, silver, or darkened metal and are especially suited to ornaments depicting leaves, trees, flames, suns, branching vines, and other motifs associated with nature, vitality, antiquity, and transformation.

In many cultures, red fossilized ferns are associated with antiquity, vitality, endurance, transformation, memory, and the persistence of life through time. Druids, herbalists, scholars, dwarven miners, natural philosophers, and explorers sometimes collect these fossils as tangible evidence of forests that flourished in ages long before recorded history. Druids may interpret a delicate plant preserved in red stone as a symbol of life's vitality leaving an enduring mark upon the earth, while dwarven traditions may associate its iron-rich coloration with the mineral forces that transformed ancient vegetation into stone. Some cultures regard the combination of a preserved plant and blood-red coloration as a symbol of the living world's ability to endure through destruction, death, and profound change. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though red fossilized ferns are favored components or decorations for enchanted items concerned with plants, earth, vitality, endurance, transformation, memory, or creatures and environments of the distant past.
