It is a group of complex boron silicate minerals that commonly form in granite pegmatites, metamorphic rocks, and hydrothermal environments. Tourmaline occurs in nearly every color imaginable, including black, blue, green, red, pink, orange, yellow, brown, violet, and colorless varieties, with some crystals displaying multiple colors within a single specimen. Its coloration is produced by varying combinations of trace elements such as iron, manganese, chromium, vanadium, copper, lithium, and others within the crystal structure. Fine specimens may exhibit exceptional transparency, vivid coloration, strong pleochroism, or striking internal zoning. When expertly cut and polished, tourmaline develops a brilliant vitreous luster and a distinctive sparkle that can range from soft and elegant to intensely vibrant, resembling captured rainbows, living flame, forest light, ocean depths, or fragments of elemental energy preserved within crystal.

Jewelers, collectors, nobles, scholars, artisans, and magical craftsmen prize tourmaline for its unparalleled variety, durability, unique crystal forms, and ability to display colors rarely found in other gemstones. Exceptional crystals may be preserved in their natural elongated prismatic form for collectors, scholars, temples, or arcane displays. Particularly valued examples include intensely colored varieties, large transparent crystals, multicolored specimens, and crystals displaying dramatic color transitions such as watermelon, bi-color, and tri-color tourmalines. Tourmaline is frequently mounted in gold, platinum, silver, electrum, bronze, copper, or elaborate settings and is especially suited to ornaments depicting elemental symbols, dragons, serpents, stars, forests, oceans, flames, storms, and other motifs associated with the forces of nature and the mysteries of creation.

homebrew.name: Brown-Green Garnet
homebrew.desc:
Brown-Green Garnet

Brown-green garnet is an uncommon and distinctive variety of garnet distinguished by earthy shades of olive green, moss green, yellow-green, bronze-green, and warm brown. Its coloration may range from subtle greenish brown tones to richer combinations of forest green and golden brown, often with complex internal color variations that become more apparent as the gemstone is turned in the light. Fine specimens are transparent to translucent and may contain minute crystalline inclusions, delicate fractures, or internal zones of contrasting color that contribute to their depth and character. When expertly cut and polished, brown-green garnet develops a bright glassy luster and lively brilliance, producing flashes of green, gold, bronze, and brown that give the gemstone an appearance reminiscent of ancient forests, fertile earth, and mineral-rich stone.

Jewelers, artisans, collectors, and nobles value brown-green garnet for its unusual coloration, durability, natural brilliance, and connection to the earth. Transparent specimens are commonly faceted into gemstones for rings, pendants, earrings, brooches, circlets, signet ornaments, and ceremonial jewelry, while more included or opaque material may be fashioned into cabochons, beads, amulets, seals, decorative inlays, and small ornamental carvings. Specimens possessing strong green coloration, attractive brown undertones, excellent transparency, and lively internal reflections are particularly desirable. Brown-green garnet is frequently mounted in gold, bronze, copper, electrum, or silver and is especially suited to ornaments depicting leaves, trees, mountains, roots, serpents, dragons, and other motifs associated with earth, nature, endurance, and hidden wealth.

In many cultures, brown-green garnet is associated with stability, growth, prosperity, resilience, patience, and the enduring strength of the natural world. Miners, merchants, druids, farmers, explorers, and craftspeople sometimes carry polished stones as symbols of steady progress and rewards gained through perseverance. Agricultural communities may associate its mingled green and brown coloration with fertile soil, healthy crops, and the cycle of renewal, while merchants may regard particularly fine specimens as tokens of prosperity built through careful planning rather than sudden fortune.

Dwarven traditions often esteem brown-green garnet as a gemstone reflecting the union of living growth and the ancient stone beneath the mountains. Prospectors may regard specimens with rich green coloration and golden-brown undertones as favorable signs of valuable mineral deposits nearby, while stoneworkers may appreciate the gemstone as a reminder that the earth's greatest treasures often require patience and careful discovery. Some druidic traditions interpret the gemstone's colors as a symbol of harmony between forest and soil, representing the balance between roots that reach into the earth and branches that seek the sky. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though brown-green garnet is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with earth, plants, prosperity, endurance, protection, vitality, or the discovery of hidden mineral wealth.
homebrew.unid:
Garnet

Garnet is a diverse family of gemstones renowned for its rich colors, strong brilliance, and excellent durability. Although deep red is its most familiar coloration, garnet occurs naturally in a remarkable range of hues including crimson, burgundy, reddish brown, orange, yellow, green, purple, pink, and nearly black, with some rare varieties displaying unusual color changes under different illumination. Fine specimens are transparent to translucent and possess a bright glassy luster, while darker stones may appear nearly opaque until held before a strong light. Garnet crystals commonly form well-defined rounded or many-faced shapes within their host rock, and exceptionally clear material can produce brilliant faceted gemstones with intense, saturated color. When expertly cut and polished, fine garnet displays a lively internal brilliance that can make richly colored stones appear to glow from within.

Jewelers prize garnet for its broad range of colors, durability, brilliance, and suitability for nearly every form of jewelry. Transparent gem-quality material is commonly faceted for rings, necklaces, earrings, brooches, circlets, crowns, bracelets, and ceremonial ornaments, while translucent or heavily included material may be fashioned into cabochons, beads, amulets, seals, and small carvings. Specimens possessing vivid coloration, strong transparency, substantial size, unusual hues, or distinctive optical effects are particularly valuable. Garnets are frequently mounted in gold, silver, platinum, electrum, bronze, or other metals chosen to complement the gemstone's coloration and are especially suited to ornaments depicting flames, hearts, shields, flowers, eyes, stars, and other motifs associated with vitality, devotion, courage, and protection.

In many cultures, garnet is associated with vitality, courage, loyalty, protection, passion, friendship, and perseverance. Warriors, travelers, nobles, merchants, priests, and adventurers sometimes wear garnets as symbols of steadfastness and the strength to endure hardship or separation. Deep red varieties may be associated with blood, life, and martial courage, while green and golden varieties may symbolize prosperity, renewal, or good fortune. Some traditions regard garnets exchanged between companions as promises of loyalty or eventual reunion, making them popular stones for friendship tokens, betrothal jewelry, and gifts carried on long journeys. Dwarven jewelers may particularly admire garnet crystals for their rich colors and naturally geometric forms, while human and elven courts frequently incorporate exceptional specimens into prestigious jewelry and ceremonial regalia. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though garnet is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with protection, courage, vitality, endurance, fire, loyalty, or resistance to fear and physical hardship.

homebrew.name: Brownish-Yellow Chrysoberyl
homebrew.desc:
Brownish-Yellow Chrysoberyl

Brownish-yellow chrysoberyl is an attractive variety of chrysoberyl distinguished by warm shades of golden brown, honey yellow, amber, ochre, and yellow-brown coloration. Its hues may appear evenly distributed or occur in subtle zones, with some specimens revealing olive, bronze, or faint green undertones as the gemstone is turned beneath changing light. Fine gem-quality stones are transparent and possess excellent clarity, while others may contain fine needles, wispy veils, crystalline inclusions, or internal zoning that adds depth and character to their warm coloration. When expertly faceted and polished, brownish-yellow chrysoberyl develops a brilliant glassy luster, producing lively flashes of gold, bronze, and rich yellow that enhance its refined and earthy appearance.

Jewelers, artisans, collectors, and craftsmen value brownish-yellow chrysoberyl for its durability, brilliance, unusual warmth of color, and connection to both precious metals and natural earth tones. Transparent specimens are commonly faceted into gemstones for rings, pendants, earrings, brooches, circlets, signet ornaments, and ceremonial jewelry, while more heavily included material may be fashioned into cabochons, beads, amulets, seals, decorative inlays, and small ornamental carvings. Specimens possessing exceptional clarity, strong brilliance, and a harmonious balance of golden-yellow and brown hues are particularly desirable. Brownish-yellow chrysoberyl is frequently mounted in gold, bronze, copper, or electrum and is especially suited to ornaments depicting suns, lions, wheat, coins, shields, crowns, and other motifs associated with prosperity, authority, steadfastness, and earned success.

In many cultures, brownish-yellow chrysoberyl is associated with prosperity, perseverance, vigilance, practical wisdom, sound judgment, and rewards earned through patient effort. Merchants, administrators, miners, explorers, and adventurers sometimes carry polished stones as symbols of careful planning, reliable decision-making, and the ability to recognize valuable opportunities hidden among ordinary circumstances. Dwarven traditions may associate its mingled gold and earth tones with precious metals concealed within common stone, viewing it as an emblem of the patient labor required to uncover true wealth. Merchant guilds and craftsmen may regard the gemstone as a reminder that lasting prosperity comes from discipline, preparation, and skill rather than simple fortune. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though brownish-yellow chrysoberyl is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with prosperity, perception, endurance, mental fortitude, practical wisdom, or the discovery of hidden wealth.
homebrew.unid:
Chrysoberyl

Chrysoberyl is a durable and brilliant gemstone distinguished by shades of pale yellow, golden yellow, yellow-green, olive, and greenish brown coloration. It is prized for its exceptional hardness, remarkable durability, and attractive natural brilliance. Fine specimens are transparent and possess a bright glassy luster, while lesser stones may contain fine needles, wispy veils, crystalline inclusions, or subtle internal zoning that adds depth and character. Some exceptional chrysoberyls display striking optical phenomena, including a sharp band of reflected light resembling the slit pupil of a cat's eye, while other rare specimens exhibit noticeable color changes when viewed under different sources of illumination. When expertly faceted and polished, transparent chrysoberyl displays excellent brilliance, producing lively flashes of yellow, green, and gold that enhance its natural beauty.

Jewelers, artisans, collectors, and craftsmen value chrysoberyl for its combination of strength, clarity, brilliance, and unusual optical effects. Transparent specimens are commonly faceted into gemstones for rings, pendants, earrings, brooches, circlets, crowns, and ceremonial jewelry, while stones displaying distinctive optical phenomena are usually cut as cabochons to best reveal their unique qualities. Specimens possessing exceptional clarity, vivid coloration, strong golden hues, or pronounced natural effects are particularly desirable. Chrysoberyl is frequently mounted in gold, platinum, electrum, or silver and is especially suited to ornaments depicting eyes, suns, lions, shields, crowns, and other motifs associated with vigilance, authority, resilience, and protection.

In many cultures, chrysoberyl is associated with protection, vigilance, confidence, prosperity, strength of will, and the recognition of hidden opportunities. Merchants, rulers, guards, explorers, and adventurers sometimes carry polished stones as symbols of alertness and the ability to perceive dangers or advantages before others notice them. Some traditions regard exceptionally clear golden specimens as tokens of prosperity and wise leadership, while stones displaying eye-like bands are considered symbols of supernatural awareness, guardianship, and protection against unseen threats. Scholars and strategists may value the gemstone as an emblem of careful observation, foresight, and disciplined judgment. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though chrysoberyl is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with perception, protection, prosperity, mental fortitude, vigilance, or resistance to surprise, deception, and hidden dangers.

homebrew.name: Cat's Eye Chrysoberyl
homebrew.desc:
Cat's Eye Chrysoberyl

Cat's eye chrysoberyl is a highly prized variety of chrysoberyl distinguished by a remarkable optical phenomenon known as chatoyancy, in which a narrow band of reflected light appears to glide across the surface of the stone like the slit pupil of a cat's eye. This effect is created by fine parallel inclusions within the gemstone that reflect light in a concentrated line, producing the appearance of a moving eye as the stone is rotated. Its body color ranges from pale yellow and honey gold to yellow-green, olive, brownish yellow, and deep golden brown. Fine specimens display a sharp, bright eye centered against an evenly colored background, with the luminous band appearing to open, close, or shift across the surface as the gemstone moves beneath a light source. When carefully polished as a cabochon, cat's eye chrysoberyl develops a smooth glassy luster that dramatically enhances this distinctive optical effect.

Jewelers, collectors, and craftsmen value cat's eye chrysoberyl for its exceptional durability, rarity, and extraordinary natural phenomenon. Unlike transparent chrysoberyl, which is commonly faceted, cat's eye chrysoberyl is almost always cut as a rounded cabochon because faceting would diminish or destroy the characteristic eye. It is commonly fashioned into rings, pendants, brooches, amulets, signet ornaments, seals, and ceremonial jewelry. Specimens possessing a sharp, continuous eye, strong contrast between the luminous band and surrounding stone, rich honey or golden coloration, and excellent polish are particularly desirable. Cat's eye chrysoberyl is frequently mounted in gold, platinum, electrum, or silver and is especially suited to ornaments depicting eyes, cats, lions, moons, guardians, sentinels, and other motifs associated with vigilance, awareness, and protection.

In many cultures, cat's eye chrysoberyl is associated with vigilance, protection, foresight, good fortune, awareness, and the detection of hidden danger. Guards, rulers, merchants, scouts, explorers, and adventurers sometimes carry polished stones as symbols of alertness and the ability to recognize threats before they become apparent. Some traditions regard the moving band of light as a watchful spirit that never sleeps, while others interpret the gemstone as a symbol of seeing through deception and uncovering what others attempt to conceal. Thieves, spies, and secret agents may value the stone in legends as an emblem of observing unseen movements while remaining unnoticed themselves. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though cat's eye chrysoberyl is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with perception, protection, darkvision, detection of invisible creatures, vigilance, or resistance to surprise, illusions, and deception.

homebrew.name: Clear Garnet
homebrew.desc:
Clear Garnet

Clear garnet is an exceptionally pale and transparent variety of garnet distinguished by an almost colorless appearance, sometimes possessing faint undertones of champagne, gray, pink, yellow, or green. Truly colorless garnet is exceptionally uncommon, since the trace elements responsible for the many familiar garnet varieties usually impart at least some visible coloration. Fine specimens possess excellent transparency and a bright glassy luster, allowing light to pass freely through the stone and produce brilliant internal reflections. Natural crystals commonly form well-defined many-faced shapes, though exceptionally clear material suitable for cutting is considerably rarer than colored garnet. When expertly faceted and polished, clear garnet can display strong brilliance and sharp flashes of white or spectral light, giving fine stones an appearance reminiscent of exceptionally clear quartz or diamond while retaining garnet's characteristic density and luster.

Jewelers prize clear garnet for its rarity, brilliance, unusual absence of strong coloration, and suitability for elegant jewelry. Transparent gem-quality material is commonly faceted for rings, pendants, earrings, brooches, circlets, crowns, and ceremonial ornaments, while specimens with attractive inclusions may be fashioned into cabochons, beads, amulets, seals, or small decorative objects. Stones possessing exceptional transparency, minimal visible inclusions, substantial size, strong brilliance, and little or no perceptible coloration are particularly valuable. Clear garnet is frequently mounted in silver, platinum, electrum, white gold, or yellow gold and is especially suited to ornaments depicting stars, eyes, prisms, snowflakes, flames, and other motifs associated with clarity, illumination, purity, and steadfastness.

In many cultures, clear garnet is associated with clarity, truth, loyalty, protection, purity of purpose, and unwavering resolve. Scholars, judges, priests, diplomats, knights, and adventurers sometimes wear clear garnets as symbols of intentions unclouded by deception or uncertainty. Some traditions regard the unusual absence of garnet's customary strong coloration as representing passion and strength brought under perfect discipline, while dwarven gemcutters may consider exceptionally clear crystals rare demonstrations of the purity attainable within minerals formed deep beneath the earth. Nobles and religious orders may incorporate particularly flawless specimens into ceremonial regalia intended to symbolize honesty, impartial judgment, or devotion to an unchanging ideal. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though clear garnet is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with protection, truth, mental clarity, courage, resistance to deception, purification, or the detection of illusions and concealed influences.

homebrew.name: Coral
homebrew.desc:
Coral

Coral is an organic gemstone formed from the skeletal remains of marine coral colonies and prized for its vivid coloration, smooth texture, and connection to the oceans. Unlike crystalline minerals, coral develops as branching or rounded structures composed primarily of calcium carbonate, with colors ranging from pale white and cream to pink, salmon, orange, red, and deep crimson. Fine specimens possess a dense, even coloration and a smooth surface texture, while natural formations may retain delicate branching shapes, growth patterns, or subtle variations that reveal their origin beneath the waves. When carefully polished, coral develops a smooth, waxy-to-glassy luster that enhances its warm coloration and organic beauty.

Jewelers and ornamental carvers value coral for its distinctive appearance, rarity, and symbolic connection to life beneath the sea. It is commonly fashioned into beads, necklaces, bracelets, rings, pendants, amulets, brooches, decorative inlays, figurines, ritual objects, and small carvings. Natural branches and unusual formations are often preserved intact as collector's pieces, while particularly fine material is polished into cabochons or carefully carved into intricate designs. Specimens possessing rich, even coloration, large size, strong surface polish, and well-preserved natural structures are particularly desirable. Coral is frequently mounted in gold, silver, bronze, copper, or electrum and is especially suited to ornaments depicting waves, shells, fish, serpents, sea creatures, ships, and other motifs associated with the ocean and life-giving waters.

In many cultures, coral is associated with protection, vitality, safe travel, fertility, healing, and the enduring power of life. Sailors, fishermen, merchants, and coastal peoples sometimes carry polished coral as a symbol of safe journeys and protection against the dangers of the sea. Healers and midwives may value red or pink coral as an emblem of vitality, renewal, and the continuation of life, while religious traditions may incorporate coral into sacred objects representing blessing, abundance, and connection to benevolent sea spirits.

Elven and coastal traditions may regard coral as a gift from the living oceans, representing harmony between land and sea and the interconnectedness of all living things. Dwarven craftsmen may appreciate coral as an unusual treasure not carved from stone but shaped by countless generations of tiny creatures, viewing it as a reminder that patience and cooperation can create wonders equal to those produced by the deepest mines. Some sailors' traditions interpret branching coral formations as natural guardians of the sea, while scholars may regard exceptionally formed specimens as records of ancient oceans and vanished environments. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though coral is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with protection, healing, vitality, water, safe travel, fertility, or communication with aquatic creatures and spirits.

homebrew.name: Dark Green Jade

The name traditionally encompasses two distinct minerals, jadeite and nephrite, both valued for their exceptional resistance to breaking and their ability to take a beautiful polish. Although rich green is its most famous coloration, jade may also occur in white, cream, gray, yellow, brown, orange, red, lavender, blue-green, and nearly black varieties, as well as mottled or multicolored combinations. Fine jade ranges from opaque to highly translucent and may possess a waxy, silky, or softly glassy luster. Jewelers and ornamental carvers prize jade for its beauty, durability, distinctive texture, and extraordinary suitability for detailed carving. Fine material is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, pendants, earrings, bracelets, rings, brooches, amulets, seals, hair ornaments, belt fittings, and ceremonial jewelry, while larger pieces may be carved into figurines, animals, flowers, religious objects, vessels, plaques, weapon fittings, and elaborate decorative objects. Jade is frequently mounted in gold, silver, platinum, electrum, bronze, or carved wooden settings and is especially suited to ornaments depicting dragons, serpents, flowers, leaves, birds, lions, clouds, and other motifs associated with prosperity, longevity, authority, and protection.

In many cultures, jade is associated with prosperity, longevity, wisdom, harmony, protection, virtue, and enduring authority. homebrew.name: Golden Pearl
homebrew.desc:
Golden Pearl

Golden pearl is a rare and highly prized variety of pearl distinguished by warm shades of pale champagne, soft yellow, rich gold, and deep metallic golden hues. Formed within certain marine mollusks, particularly large tropical oysters, golden pearls acquire their coloration from the natural pigments within their nacre layers. Their colors may range from a delicate ivory-gold glow to an intense, saturated golden sheen, with fine specimens displaying thick nacre, exceptional smoothness, and a deep orient that creates a luminous radiance beneath the surface. When carefully polished, golden pearl develops a soft, silky-to-waxy luster that enhances its warmth and gives the gemstone an appearance reminiscent of sunlight captured within a living jewel.

Jewelers, nobles, and collectors prize golden pearl for its rarity, natural beauty, warm coloration, and association with luxury and refinement. It is commonly fashioned into necklaces, earrings, pendants, rings, bracelets, brooches, circlets, crowns, ceremonial ornaments, amulets, and decorative inlays. Particularly desirable specimens possess rich golden coloration, thick nacre, strong luster, symmetrical forms, and an intense inner glow. Golden pearls are frequently mounted in gold, electrum, platinum, bronze, or silver and are especially suited to ornaments depicting suns, crowns, lions, flowers, wheat, coins, and other motifs associated with wealth, nobility, abundance, and divine favor.

In many cultures, golden pearl is associated with prosperity, wisdom, authority, generosity, enlightenment, and the rewards of patience. Rulers, merchants, priests, diplomats, and wealthy patrons sometimes wear golden pearls as symbols of cultivated power, good fortune, and prosperity gained through careful stewardship. Coastal societies may regard them as treasures gifted by the sea, while agricultural communities may associate their golden coloration with ripened grain, plentiful harvests, and the blessings of the sun. Some traditions view the pearl's formation over years within a living creature as a symbol of patience, transformation, and the creation of beauty from adversity.

Elven cultures may regard golden pearls as expressions of harmony between the ocean and the natural world, valuing their gentle radiance as a reflection of sunlight upon calm waters. Dwarven artisans may admire them as treasures shaped through endurance and hidden labor, comparing the slow creation of a pearl to the careful refinement required in master craftsmanship. Some royal traditions reserve especially magnificent golden pearls for crowns, ceremonial robes, and sacred objects, believing their radiance reflects wisdom tempered by compassion. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though golden pearl is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with prosperity, leadership, wisdom, sunlight, healing, water, protection, or the creation of harmony among allies.

Perfectly spherical pearls with smooth surfaces, strong orient, large size, rare coloration, and exceptional luster are among the most desirable, though baroque pearls with unusual shapes resembling animals, faces, flowers, or symbols may also command great admiration. Pearls are frequently set in gold, silver, platinum, electrum, ivory, shell, coral, or carved wood and are especially suited to ornaments depicting moons, waves, seashells, swans, mermaids, dragons, stars, and other motifs associated with beauty, water, purity, and hidden treasures.

In many cultures, pearls are associated with purity, wisdom, prosperity, protection, transformation, and the mysteries of the sea. homebrew.name: Golden Yellow Amber

homebrew.name: Golden-Green Chrome Diopside

homebrew.name: Gray Kyanite
homebrew.desc:
Gray Kyanite

Gray kyanite is a distinctive variety of kyanite characterized by subdued gray coloration and the elongated, bladelike crystal forms typical of the mineral. Its hues range from pale silver-gray and dove gray to slate, smoky gray, and deep charcoal, sometimes accompanied by subtle blue, green, brown, or silvery undertones. Natural specimens commonly form flattened blades or elongated crystals marked by pronounced lengthwise striations, and some occur as radiating clusters or overlapping formations resembling feathers, spearheads, or narrow sword blades. Individual crystal faces may possess a glassy to pearly luster that produces soft silver reflections when turned beneath the light. Kyanite possesses the unusual characteristic of having markedly different hardness depending upon the direction in which it is tested, making its crystals challenging to cut and polish without splitting. Fine gray specimens are therefore valued both as ornamental material and in their natural crystalline form, particularly when they possess well-defined blades, attractive luster, even coloration, and minimal damage.

Jewelers, collectors, mineralogists, and ornamental carvers prize gray kyanite for its understated coloration, distinctive bladed structure, unusual physical properties, and elegant natural appearance. Transparent or translucent gem-quality material may be carefully faceted for pendants, earrings, brooches, rings, circlets, and ceremonial jewelry, while more opaque material can be fashioned into cabochons, beads, amulets, polished blades, seals, and small decorative objects. Particularly attractive natural crystals and radiating clusters are often preserved largely unaltered and incorporated into pendants, ritual ornaments, mineral displays, or jewelry designed to emphasize their natural form. Specimens possessing attractive silver-gray coloration, strong surface luster, sharply defined blades, substantial size, unusual radiating growth, or minimal fractures are particularly desirable. Gray kyanite is frequently mounted in silver, platinum, iron, steel, electrum, pewter, or darkened metal and is especially suited to ornaments depicting swords, feathers, wings, mountains, clouds, and other motifs associated with discipline, clarity, endurance, and stone.

In many cultures, gray kyanite is associated with clarity, discipline, perseverance, balance, steadfastness, and thoughtful judgment. Scholars, judges, warriors, miners, craftspeople, dwarven mineralogists, travelers, and adventurers sometimes carry gray kyanite as a symbol of remaining calm and deliberate when confronting difficult choices or uncertain circumstances. Its straight bladelike crystals may be interpreted as symbols of purpose and decisive action, while its subdued gray coloration encourages associations with stone, steel, neutrality, and judgment unclouded by passion. Its directional hardness may cause philosophers to regard it as a reminder that strength alone is insufficient without understanding how that strength should be applied. Dwarven craftsmen may particularly admire well-formed gray crystals for their resemblance to blades naturally fashioned within the earth. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though gray kyanite is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with earth, protection, mental clarity, discipline, truth, endurance, or resistance to confusion and deception.

In many cultures, kyanite is associated with clarity, discipline, direction, truth, perseverance, and focused purpose. Scholars, judges, navigators, priests, warriors, artisans, and adventurers sometimes wear kyanite as a symbol of maintaining a chosen course despite obstacles or uncertainty. Blue specimens may be associated with clear skies, deep water, or calm judgment, while dwarven mineralogists and gemcutters may particularly esteem kyanite for the technical skill required to work its difficult crystals successfully. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though kyanite is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with mental clarity, truth, navigation, discipline, divination, protection, or resistance to confusion and deception.

Chrysoberyl is a durable and brilliant gemstone distinguished by shades of pale yellow, golden yellow, yellow-green, olive, and greenish brown coloration. It is prized for its exceptional hardness, remarkable durability, and attractive natural brilliance. Fine specimens are transparent and possess a bright glassy luster, while lesser stones may contain fine needles, wispy veils, crystalline inclusions, or subtle internal zoning that adds depth and character. Some exceptional chrysoberyls display striking optical phenomena, including a sharp band of reflected light resembling the slit pupil of a cat's eye, while other rare specimens exhibit noticeable color changes when viewed under different sources of illumination. When expertly faceted and polished, transparent chrysoberyl displays excellent brilliance, producing lively flashes of yellow, green, and gold that enhance its natural beauty.

Jewelers, artisans, collectors, and craftsmen value chrysoberyl for its combination of strength, clarity, brilliance, and unusual optical effects. Transparent specimens are commonly faceted into gemstones for rings, pendants, earrings, brooches, circlets, crowns, and ceremonial jewelry, while stones displaying distinctive optical phenomena are usually cut as cabochons to best reveal their unique qualities. Specimens possessing exceptional clarity, vivid coloration, strong golden hues, or pronounced natural effects are particularly desirable. Chrysoberyl is frequently mounted in gold, platinum, electrum, or silver and is especially suited to ornaments depicting eyes, suns, lions, shields, crowns, and other motifs associated with vigilance, authority, resilience, and protection.

In many cultures, chrysoberyl is associated with protection, vigilance, confidence, prosperity, strength of will, and the recognition of hidden opportunities. Merchants, rulers, guards, explorers, and adventurers sometimes carry polished stones as symbols of alertness and the ability to perceive dangers or advantages before others notice them. Some traditions regard exceptionally clear golden specimens as tokens of prosperity and wise leadership, while stones displaying eye-like bands are considered symbols of supernatural awareness, guardianship, and protection against unseen threats. Scholars and strategists may value the gemstone as an emblem of careful observation, foresight, and disciplined judgment. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though chrysoberyl is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with perception, protection, prosperity, mental fortitude, vigilance, or resistance to surprise, deception, and hidden dangers.

homebrew.name: Green Garnet
homebrew.desc:
Green Garnet

Green garnet is a striking and often highly prized variety of garnet distinguished by coloration ranging from pale yellow-green and fresh leaf green to vivid grass green, emerald green, and deep forest green. Its color is produced by trace elements within the crystal and may be remarkably intense in exceptional specimens, with some varieties rivaling fine emerald in richness and brilliance. Fine stones are transparent to translucent and possess a bright glassy luster, while darker specimens may reveal flashes of lighter green or yellow when illuminated from behind. Natural crystals commonly form well-defined many-faced shapes and may occur embedded within contrasting pale, brown, or dark host rock. When expertly faceted and polished, transparent green garnet can display exceptional brilliance and lively flashes of green, yellow, and occasionally blue-green light, giving the finest stones a vivid and luminous appearance.

Jewelers prize green garnet for its beauty, rarity, durability, brilliance, and distinctive alternative to more familiar red garnets. Transparent gem-quality material is commonly faceted for rings, necklaces, earrings, brooches, bracelets, circlets, crowns, and ceremonial regalia, while translucent or heavily included specimens may be fashioned into cabochons, beads, amulets, seals, and small carvings. Specimens possessing vivid green coloration, excellent transparency, substantial size, strong brilliance, or particularly desirable emerald-green hues are especially valuable. Green garnet is frequently mounted in gold, platinum, electrum, silver, or bronze and is especially suited to ornaments depicting leaves, vines, flowers, trees, serpents, dragons, and other motifs associated with nature, prosperity, vitality, and renewal.

In many cultures, green garnet is associated with renewal, prosperity, vitality, growth, endurance, and good fortune. Druids, merchants, nobles, healers, elven jewelers, dwarven gemcutters, and adventurers sometimes wear green garnets as symbols of flourishing life, material abundance, and strength maintained through continual renewal. Elven traditions may particularly admire vivid green specimens for their resemblance to leaves illuminated by sunlight, while dwarven traditions may esteem them as rare examples of the colors of living forests emerging naturally from crystals formed within the deep earth. Merchants and rulers sometimes favor especially brilliant stones as symbols of increasing wealth and prosperous endeavors, while travelers may carry smaller specimens as tokens of continued vitality and eventual safe return. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though green garnet is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with plants, healing, prosperity, vitality, protection, endurance, or resistance to poison and disease.
homebrew.unid:
Garnet

Garnet is a diverse family of gemstones renowned for its rich colors, strong brilliance, and excellent durability. Although deep red is its most familiar coloration, garnet occurs naturally in a remarkable range of hues including crimson, burgundy, reddish brown, orange, yellow, green, purple, pink, and nearly black, with some rare varieties displaying unusual color changes under different illumination. Fine specimens are transparent to translucent and possess a bright glassy luster, while darker stones may appear nearly opaque until held before a strong light. Garnet crystals commonly form well-defined rounded or many-faced shapes within their host rock, and exceptionally clear material can produce brilliant faceted gemstones with intense, saturated color. When expertly cut and polished, fine garnet displays a lively internal brilliance that can make richly colored stones appear to glow from within.

Jewelers prize garnet for its broad range of colors, durability, brilliance, and suitability for nearly every form of jewelry. Transparent gem-quality material is commonly faceted for rings, necklaces, earrings, brooches, circlets, crowns, bracelets, and ceremonial ornaments, while translucent or heavily included material may be fashioned into cabochons, beads, amulets, seals, and small carvings. Specimens possessing vivid coloration, strong transparency, substantial size, unusual hues, or distinctive optical effects are particularly valuable. Garnets are frequently mounted in gold, silver, platinum, electrum, bronze, or other metals chosen to complement the gemstone's coloration and are especially suited to ornaments depicting flames, hearts, shields, flowers, eyes, stars, and other motifs associated with vitality, devotion, courage, and protection.

In many cultures, garnet is associated with vitality, courage, loyalty, protection, passion, friendship, and perseverance. Warriors, travelers, nobles, merchants, priests, and adventurers sometimes wear garnets as symbols of steadfastness and the strength to endure hardship or separation. Deep red varieties may be associated with blood, life, and martial courage, while green and golden varieties may symbolize prosperity, renewal, or good fortune. Some traditions regard garnets exchanged between companions as promises of loyalty or eventual reunion, making them popular stones for friendship tokens, betrothal jewelry, and gifts carried on long journeys. Dwarven jewelers may particularly admire garnet crystals for their rich colors and naturally geometric forms, while human and elven courts frequently incorporate exceptional specimens into prestigious jewelry and ceremonial regalia. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though garnet is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with protection, courage, vitality, endurance, fire, loyalty, or resistance to fear and physical hardship.

homebrew.name: Green Marine Pearl
homebrew.desc:
Green Marine Pearl

Green marine pearls are rare and captivating organic gemstones formed within saltwater oysters and distinguished by their unusual coloration, exceptional nacreous luster, and connection to the living waters of the sea. Unlike minerals formed through geological processes, pearls are created through biological activity as the oyster deposits successive layers of nacre around an irritant or implanted nucleus. Their colors range from pale seafoam green and mint to jade green, emerald green, olive, and deep forest green, often displaying subtle overtones of silver, blue, gold, bronze, or violet that shift beneath changing light. The finest specimens possess a deep reflective luster known as orient, created by the interaction of light with countless microscopic layers of nacre. Green marine pearls may occur in perfectly round, near-round, oval, drop, button, or irregular baroque forms, with unusual shapes sometimes prized for their individuality. Their natural coloration and soft inner glow give them an appearance reminiscent of tropical waters, emerald lagoons, underwater forests, and sunlight filtering through ocean depths.

Jewelers, nobles, priests, merchants, artisans, and collectors prize green marine pearls for their rarity, exotic coloration, organic beauty, and association with the mysteries and abundance of the sea. Fine pearls are commonly fashioned into necklaces, earrings, rings, bracelets, pendants, brooches, circlets, crowns, hair ornaments, amulets, seals, and ceremonial garments, while exceptional specimens may be preserved as royal treasures, temple offerings, legendary gifts, or magical components. Pearls possessing vivid green coloration, intense orient, smooth surfaces, large size, excellent symmetry, and attractive secondary hues are particularly desirable. Perfectly round examples are highly prized for traditional jewelry, while baroque pearls with shapes resembling leaves, shells, waves, eyes, seeds, or strange sea creatures may inspire unique works of art. Green marine pearls are frequently set in gold, silver, platinum, electrum, bronze, or carved coral and are especially suited to ornaments depicting sea serpents, merfolk, turtles, waves, coral forests, flowers, vines, and other motifs associated with nature, renewal, life, and hidden ocean treasures.

In many cultures, green marine pearls are associated with renewal, healing, fertility, prosperity, harmony, and the living power of the ocean. Sailors, druids, healers, aquatic peoples, priests, merchants, elves, nobles, and adventurers sometimes carry green marine pearls as symbols of life sustained by the waters and treasures gained through patience and respect for nature. Their green coloration and marine origin may inspire legends that they are seeds of underwater forests, tears of ocean spirits, gifts from sea deities who nurture all living things, or pearls formed where sacred currents flow through enchanted reefs. Aquatic cultures may regard exceptional green pearls as signs of favor from the depths, while druids and nature-focused traditions may associate them with the connection between ocean life, forests, and the greater cycles of the world. Merchants may view them as symbols of abundance and successful voyages, while healers may treasure them as representations of renewal and restoration. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though green marine pearls are favored components for enchanted items concerned with water, healing, nature, fertility, growth, communication with aquatic creatures, prosperity, protection, or the preservation of ancient oceanic knowledge.
homebrew.unid:
Pearl

Pearl is an organic gemstone formed when a mollusk deposits successive layers of nacre around an irritant or foreign particle within its shell. Unlike minerals formed through geological processes, pearls are created through biological activity and are composed primarily of calcium carbonate crystals bound together with organic material. Their appearance ranges from pure white and cream to pink, silver, gray, gold, blue, green, black, and many subtle combinations of these colors. The most prized pearls possess a deep, glowing luster known as orient, produced by the interaction of light with the layered structure of the nacre. Pearls may be perfectly round, near-round, oval, button-shaped, drop-shaped, baroque, or irregular, with unusual forms often valued for their individuality. When polished and carefully handled, pearls display a soft satiny glow rather than the sharp brilliance of faceted gemstones, giving them a uniquely elegant and almost living appearance.

Jewelers, nobles, priests, artisans, and collectors prize pearls for their rarity, organic origin, gentle luster, and association with refinement and status. Fine pearls are commonly fashioned into necklaces, earrings, rings, bracelets, pendants, brooches, circlets, crowns, tiaras, hair ornaments, amulets, seals, and ceremonial garments, while larger or unusually shaped pearls may be preserved as treasures, religious offerings, royal decorations, or magical components. Perfectly spherical pearls with smooth surfaces, strong orient, large size, rare coloration, and exceptional luster are among the most desirable, though baroque pearls with unusual shapes resembling animals, faces, flowers, or symbols may also command great admiration. Pearls are frequently set in gold, silver, platinum, electrum, ivory, shell, coral, or carved wood and are especially suited to ornaments depicting moons, waves, seashells, swans, mermaids, dragons, stars, and other motifs associated with beauty, water, purity, and hidden treasures.

In many cultures, pearls are associated with purity, wisdom, prosperity, protection, transformation, and the mysteries of the sea. Sailors, merchants, rulers, priests, healers, nobles, aquatic peoples, elves, and adventurers sometimes carry pearls as symbols of fortune, divine favor, and treasures drawn from hidden depths. Their creation within living creatures may inspire legends that pearls are tears of sea spirits, hardened drops of moonlight, gifts from ocean deities, or fragments of wisdom formed over many years within sacred creatures. Coastal cultures may regard exceptional pearls as offerings worthy of kings and temples, while scholars and sages may compare their gradual formation to the accumulation of knowledge through patience and experience. Elven traditions may particularly prize flawless pearls for ceremonial jewelry representing harmony between land, sea, and sky. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though pearls are favored components for enchanted items concerned with water, healing, protection, wisdom, purification, communication, dreams, transformation, or the mysteries of the deep.

homebrew.name: Green Spinel
homebrew.desc:
Green Spinel

Green spinel is a rare and distinctive variety of spinel distinguished by its natural green coloration, exceptional brilliance, and elegant gemstone character. Spinel is a magnesium aluminum oxide mineral that forms in metamorphic rocks, limestone deposits, and alluvial gemstone gravels. Its green coloration is produced by trace amounts of iron, chromium, cobalt, and other elements within the crystal structure. Green spinel ranges from pale mint green and soft sage to olive, emerald-like green, deep forest green, and bluish-green shades. Fine specimens may display excellent transparency, strong internal glow, and a lively brilliance that gives the stone a fresh, vibrant appearance. Unlike many green gemstones, green spinel combines attractive color with the durability and clarity associated with the spinel family. When expertly cut and polished, green spinel develops a brilliant vitreous luster and a sparkling appearance reminiscent of sunlit leaves, deep forests, ancient jade, or living energy captured within crystal.

Jewelers, nobles, collectors, and master artisans prize green spinel for its rarity, durability, brilliance, and unusual natural coloration. Fine material is commonly fashioned into faceted gems for rings, pendants, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, brooches, seals, ceremonial objects, and decorative jewelry, while exceptional stones may be preserved as heirlooms, diplomatic gifts, magical components, or collector treasures. Specimens possessing vivid green coloration, excellent transparency, strong brilliance, substantial size, minimal inclusions, and precise cutting are particularly desirable. Green spinel is frequently mounted in gold, platinum, silver, electrum, bronze, copper, or natural-themed settings and is especially suited to ornaments depicting leaves, forests, vines, serpents, dragons, stags, flowers, crowns, and other motifs associated with growth, renewal, prosperity, and harmony with nature.

In many cultures, green spinel is associated with renewal, vitality, harmony, prosperity, healing, and the enduring strength of the living world. Druids, healers, elves, scholars, merchants, priests, wizards, and adventurers sometimes carry green spinel as a symbol of growth, balance, and the pursuit of wisdom through connection with nature. Its green coloration may inspire legends that it formed from the hearts of ancient forests, the blessings of nature spirits, fragments of sacred groves, or the life force of the world crystallized beneath the earth. When expertly cut and polished, spinel develops a brilliant vitreous luster and a vibrant fire that rivals many of the world's most celebrated gemstones.

Jewelers, monarchs, collectors, and master artisans prize spinel for its beauty, rarity, durability, and wide range of natural colors. homebrew.name: Green Tourmaline
homebrew.desc:
Green Tourmaline

Green tourmaline is a highly admired and diverse variety of tourmaline distinguished by its rich green coloration, exceptional crystal formations, and association with growth, vitality, and the living forces of nature. It belongs to the tourmaline mineral group, a complex family of boron silicate minerals that form in granite pegmatites, metamorphic rocks, and hydrothermal environments. Green tourmaline ranges in color from pale mint and soft sage to vibrant grass green, emerald green, forest green, and deep verdant shades, with coloration produced by trace elements such as iron, chromium, vanadium, and other chemical variations within the crystal structure. Fine specimens may display strong pleochroism, revealing different shades of green depending on the angle of observation, as well as excellent transparency and internal brilliance. When expertly cut and polished, green tourmaline develops a brilliant vitreous luster and a lively sparkle reminiscent of sunlight filtering through leaves, ancient forests, emerald waters, or the concentrated essence of nature preserved within crystal.

Jewelers, collectors, nobles, artisans, and master craftsmen prize green tourmaline for its beauty, durability, range of colors, and exceptional crystal forms. Fine material is commonly fashioned into faceted gems for rings, pendants, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, brooches, seals, ceremonial objects, and decorative jewelry, while larger crystals are often preserved in their natural elongated prismatic form for collectors, scholars, and arcane displays. Specimens possessing vivid green coloration, excellent transparency, strong brilliance, attractive pleochroism, substantial size, and minimal inclusions are particularly desirable. Chromium-rich and intensely colored green tourmalines are especially valued for their resemblance to fine emeralds. Green tourmaline is frequently mounted in gold, platinum, silver, electrum, bronze, or natural-themed settings and is especially suited to ornaments depicting leaves, vines, forests, trees, stags, serpents, dragons, flowers, and other motifs associated with renewal, harmony, fertility, and the hidden power of the natural world.

In many cultures, green tourmaline is associated with growth, healing, renewal, prosperity, harmony, vitality, and the enduring strength of life. Druids, healers, elves, rangers, scholars, priests, wizards, merchants, and adventurers sometimes carry green tourmaline as a symbol of balance, restoration, and connection to the living world. Its verdant coloration may inspire legends that it formed from the first leaves of the world tree, the hearts of ancient forests, the blessings of nature spirits, or fragments of the life force that flows through all creatures. Druids may regard it as a representation of nature's cycles and the harmony between all living things, while healers may associate it with renewal and restored strength. Merchants may value it as a token of flourishing ventures and abundance, while scholars may study it as an example of the earth's ability to preserve the beauty of life within mineral form. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though green tourmaline is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with healing, nature, prosperity, growth, protection, vitality, communication with natural creatures, fertility, transformation, or restoring balance between civilization and the wild.
homebrew.unid:
Tourmaline

Tourmaline is one of the most diverse and remarkable gemstone families, celebrated for its extraordinary range of colors, complex crystal structures, natural beauty, and association with elemental forces. It is a group of complex boron silicate minerals that commonly form in granite pegmatites, metamorphic rocks, and hydrothermal environments. Tourmaline occurs in nearly every color imaginable, including black, blue, green, red, pink, orange, yellow, brown, violet, and colorless varieties, with some crystals displaying multiple colors within a single specimen. Its coloration is produced by varying combinations of trace elements such as iron, manganese, chromium, vanadium, copper, lithium, and others within the crystal structure. Fine specimens may exhibit exceptional transparency, vivid coloration, strong pleochroism, or striking internal zoning. When expertly cut and polished, tourmaline develops a brilliant vitreous luster and a distinctive sparkle that can range from soft and elegant to intensely vibrant, resembling captured rainbows, living flame, forest light, ocean depths, or fragments of elemental energy preserved within crystal.

Jewelers, collectors, nobles, scholars, artisans, and magical craftsmen prize tourmaline for its unparalleled variety, durability, unique crystal forms, and ability to display colors rarely found in other gemstones. Fine material is commonly fashioned into faceted gems for rings, pendants, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, brooches, circlets, seals, and ceremonial jewelry, while opaque or patterned varieties are frequently carved into cabochons, beads, figurines, amulets, and decorative objects. Exceptional crystals may be preserved in their natural elongated prismatic form for collectors, scholars, temples, or arcane displays. Particularly valued examples include intensely colored varieties, large transparent crystals, multicolored specimens, and crystals displaying dramatic color transitions such as watermelon, bi-color, and tri-color tourmalines. Tourmaline is frequently mounted in gold, platinum, silver, electrum, bronze, copper, or elaborate settings and is especially suited to ornaments depicting elemental symbols, dragons, serpents, stars, forests, oceans, flames, storms, and other motifs associated with the forces of nature and the mysteries of creation.

In many cultures, tourmaline is associated with balance, transformation, protection, creativity, elemental harmony, and the infinite variety of the natural world. Wizards, scholars, artisans, druids, priests, nobles, healers, and adventurers sometimes carry tourmaline as a symbol of adaptability, discovery, and the connection between all forms of energy. Its incredible range of colors may inspire legends that it contains fragments of every element, that it was created where the forces of earth, sky, fire, and water met, or that ancient spirits gifted the world with crystals reflecting every aspect of existence. Different colors are often associated with different qualities: black tourmaline with protection, green with growth, blue with wisdom, red and pink with vitality and compassion, and multicolored varieties with balance and transformation. Scholars may value tourmaline as a natural wonder demonstrating the complexity of the world, while artisans may regard it as a symbol of imagination and limitless possibility. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though tourmaline is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with elemental forces, protection, transformation, creativity, energy manipulation, harmony, magical research, communication with nature, or channeling the diverse powers of the world.

homebrew.name: Green Zincite

Green Zincite

Green zincite is an exceptionally rare and unusual variety of zincite distinguished by its green coloration, crystalline brilliance, and connection to the transformative forces of the earth. Zincite is a zinc oxide mineral that forms naturally in zinc deposits, particularly in environments where zinc-bearing minerals undergo oxidation and chemical alteration. While natural zincite is most commonly known for its vivid red, orange, and yellow varieties, green zincite is extremely uncommon and may occur through the influence of trace elements, mineral inclusions, or unusual geological conditions during formation. Its colors range from pale mint green and yellow-green to olive, emerald-like green, and deep forest-green shades. Fine specimens may display translucent areas, internal glow, or subtle variations in tone that enhance their rarity and beauty. When expertly polished, green zincite develops a brilliant resinous to adamantine luster and an appearance reminiscent of emerald fire, ancient forest crystals, glowing moss, or a fragment of living energy preserved within mineral form.

Jewelers, collectors, scholars, artisans, and magical craftsmen prize green zincite for its extreme rarity, unusual coloration, fragile beauty, and distinctive place among zincite varieties. Because zincite is relatively soft and delicate compared to many gemstones, green zincite is generally reserved for collectors, protected jewelry pieces, ceremonial objects, and arcane treasures rather than everyday wear. Fine material may be fashioned into carefully protected cabochons, pendants, earrings, rings, brooches, seals, amulets, magical foci, decorative carvings, and display specimens. Crystals possessing vivid natural green coloration, strong luster, excellent transparency, well-formed crystal structures, substantial size, and minimal fractures are particularly desirable. Green zincite is frequently mounted in gold, silver, platinum, bronze, copper, electrum, or nature-inspired settings and is especially suited to ornaments depicting leaves, trees, serpents, dragons, forests, vines, springs, and other motifs associated with growth, renewal, healing, and the hidden powers of nature.

homebrew.name: Jade
homebrew.desc:
Jade

Jade is a highly prized ornamental gemstone renowned for its toughness, smooth texture, and broad range of colors. The name traditionally encompasses two distinct minerals, jadeite and nephrite, both valued for their exceptional resistance to breaking and their ability to take a beautiful polish. Although rich green is its most famous coloration, jade may also occur in white, cream, gray, yellow, brown, orange, red, lavender, blue-green, and nearly black varieties, as well as mottled or multicolored combinations. Fine jade ranges from opaque to highly translucent and may possess a waxy, silky, or softly glassy luster. The most desirable specimens combine attractive, evenly distributed coloration with fine texture and good translucency, creating a deep luminous appearance when polished. Because jade is exceptionally tough rather than merely hard, even relatively delicate carvings can survive handling that might fracture more brittle gemstones.

Jewelers and ornamental carvers prize jade for its beauty, durability, distinctive texture, and extraordinary suitability for detailed carving. Fine material is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, pendants, earrings, bracelets, rings, brooches, amulets, seals, hair ornaments, belt fittings, and ceremonial jewelry, while larger pieces may be carved into figurines, animals, flowers, religious objects, vessels, plaques, weapon fittings, and elaborate decorative objects. Specimens possessing vivid coloration, strong translucency, uniform texture, substantial size, attractive mottling, or unusual natural patterns are particularly valuable. Jade's exceptional toughness allows skilled artisans to create thin pierced designs, intricate reliefs, and finely detailed carvings that would be hazardous in many more brittle gemstones. Jade is frequently mounted in gold, silver, platinum, electrum, bronze, or carved wooden settings and is especially suited to ornaments depicting dragons, serpents, flowers, leaves, birds, lions, clouds, and other motifs associated with prosperity, longevity, authority, and protection.

In many cultures, jade is associated with prosperity, longevity, wisdom, harmony, protection, virtue, and enduring authority. Rulers, nobles, priests, scholars, merchants, warriors, healers, and wealthy adventurers sometimes wear jade as a symbol of status combined with disciplined character and lasting strength. homebrew.name: Jet
homebrew.desc:
Jet

Jet is a lightweight, organic gemstone formed from ancient wood that was buried, compressed, and chemically altered over immense spans of geological time. Although often mistaken for a black mineral, jet originates from plant material and is closely related to certain forms of lignite coal. Its coloration ranges from deep brownish black to intense, nearly uniform black, with fine specimens possessing a smooth surface and rich coloration free from obvious cracks or dull inclusions. Freshly worked jet may display a soft resinous or waxy luster, while carefully polished material can develop a brilliant glossy surface resembling black glass. Despite this appearance, jet is considerably lighter and softer than most dark gemstones, making even relatively large pieces comfortable to wear. Fine material can be carved with considerable detail, though its softness requires careful workmanship to avoid scratches, chips, or damage.

Jewelers and ornamental carvers prize jet for its intense black coloration, light weight, ability to take a fine polish, and exceptional suitability for carving. Fine material is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, pendants, earrings, bracelets, brooches, rings, amulets, seals, hair ornaments, buttons, rosaries, and decorative inlays, while larger pieces may be carved into cameos, figurines, plaques, miniature portraits, religious objects, and other intricate ornaments. Because jet is lightweight, elaborate necklaces and large carved ornaments can be produced without the burdensome weight associated with similarly sized pieces of stone. Specimens possessing deep uniform black coloration, compact structure, substantial size, minimal fractures, and a brilliant polish are particularly desirable. Jet is frequently mounted in silver, gold, platinum, electrum, pewter, or darkened metal and is especially suited to ornaments depicting ravens, roses, skulls, moons, serpents, mourning figures, and other motifs associated with night, remembrance, solemnity, and mystery.

In many cultures, jet is associated with mourning, protection, remembrance, dignity, mystery, and the enduring memory of the dead. Priests, mourners, nobles, widows, scholars, travelers, undertakers, and adventurers sometimes wear jet as a symbol of grief respectfully borne and memories preserved after death. Its origin as ancient wood transformed into a glossy black material may cause druids and natural philosophers to regard it as an unusual union of life, earth, and immense spans of time, while funerary traditions may incorporate carved jet into mourning jewelry, memorial tokens, reliquaries, and ornaments placed with the deceased. Its deep black coloration also encourages associations with night, secrecy, and protection from unseen dangers. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though jet is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with protection, darkness, memory, death, spirits, concealment, or resistance to fear and hostile supernatural influences.

homebrew.name: Lanvender Charoite
homebrew.desc:
Lavender Charoite

Lavender charoite is a rare and captivating variety of charoite distinguished by delicate shades of lavender, pale violet, lilac, and soft purple coloration. It is an ornamental gemstone composed of complex silicate minerals, renowned for its swirling fibrous structure and dramatic natural patterns. Its coloration may appear as gentle lavender fields, flowing violet streaks, or intricate mixtures of purple and pale tones interwoven with streaks or patches of white, gray, black, and occasional golden brown. Fine specimens often display flowing, featherlike, or cloudlike patterns created by the stone's fibrous structure, with some pieces exhibiting a subtle silky sheen or chatoyant effect that shifts as the gem is turned beneath the light. When carefully polished, lavender charoite develops a smooth glassy-to-pearly luster that enhances its graceful patterns and gives the stone an almost fluid, dreamlike appearance.

Jewelers, ornamental artisans, collectors, and craftsmen value lavender charoite for its rarity, distinctive coloration, and highly individual natural markings. It is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, pendants, brooches, amulets, decorative inlays, figurines, seals, and small ornamental carvings. Because of its complex patterns, each piece is often considered unique, with artisans carefully shaping the stone to highlight its swirling designs and internal movement. Specimens possessing vivid lavender coloration, graceful flowing patterns, strong translucency, or a pronounced silky sheen are particularly desirable. Lavender charoite is frequently mounted in silver, platinum, electrum, or pale gold and is especially suited to ornaments depicting spirals, stars, moons, eyes, feathers, dragons, and other motifs associated with transformation, mystery, intuition, and mystical power.

In many cultures, lavender charoite is associated with transformation, courage, intuition, spiritual insight, emotional resilience, and mastery over fear. homebrew.name: Light Green Jade

Light Green Jade

Natural examples may display subtle clouds, wispy veins, faint mottling, or gradual variations between pale and slightly deeper shades of green, while exceptionally uniform specimens are particularly desirable. The stone's lighter coloration often makes internal patterns and variations more readily visible than in darker varieties. homebrew.name: Lilac Tourmaline

Lilac Tourmaline

Lilac tourmaline is a rare and delicate variety of tourmaline distinguished by its soft purple coloration, graceful appearance, and association with imagination, intuition, and refined beauty. It belongs to the tourmaline mineral group, a complex family of boron silicate minerals that form in granite pegmatites, metamorphic rocks, and hydrothermal environments. Lilac tourmaline ranges in color from pale lavender and soft violet to pinkish-lilac, mauve, and cool purple shades, with coloration produced by trace elements such as manganese and variations in the crystal structure. Fine specimens may display subtle pleochroism, revealing slightly different tones when viewed from different angles, as well as excellent transparency and a gentle inner glow. When expertly cut and polished, lilac tourmaline develops a brilliant vitreous luster and an elegant sparkle reminiscent of twilight skies, lavender blossoms, silk dyed with royal pigments, or a fragment of enchanted moonlight preserved within crystal.

Jewelers, nobles, collectors, artisans, and master craftsmen prize lilac tourmaline for its rarity, unusual coloration, durability, and refined visual appeal. Fine material is commonly fashioned into faceted gems for rings, pendants, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, brooches, circlets, seals, ceremonial objects, and delicate magical ornaments, while larger crystals may be preserved in their natural elongated prismatic form for collectors, scholars, and arcane displays. Specimens possessing even lilac coloration, excellent transparency, strong brilliance, attractive pleochroism, substantial size, and minimal inclusions are particularly desirable. Lilac tourmaline is frequently mounted in silver, platinum, white gold, rose gold, electrum, or delicate jeweled settings and is especially suited to ornaments depicting moons, stars, flowers, butterflies, feathers, spirits, crowns, and other motifs associated with elegance, dreams, transformation, and hidden knowledge.

In many cultures, lilac tourmaline is associated with intuition, creativity, imagination, spiritual refinement, harmony, and the quiet mysteries of the unseen world. Wizards, scholars, artists, priests, elves, healers, and adventurers sometimes carry lilac tourmaline as a symbol of inspiration, insight, and the pursuit of beauty and understanding. Its gentle coloration may inspire legends that it formed from the dreams of ancient poets, the whispers of moon spirits, the petals of celestial flowers transformed into crystal, or fragments of twilight captured by the earth. Mystics may regard it as a symbol of intuition and awareness of subtle forces, while healers may connect it with emotional balance and inner peace. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though lilac tourmaline is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with dreams, divination, creativity, illusion, communication, emotional harmony, magical research, spiritual growth, protection, or revealing truths hidden beyond ordinary perception.
homebrew.unid:
Tourmaline

Tourmaline is one of the most diverse and remarkable gemstone families, celebrated for its extraordinary range of colors, complex crystal structures, natural beauty, and association with elemental forces. It is a group of complex boron silicate minerals that commonly form in granite pegmatites, metamorphic rocks, and hydrothermal environments. Tourmaline occurs in nearly every color imaginable, including black, blue, green, red, pink, orange, yellow, brown, violet, and colorless varieties, with some crystals displaying multiple colors within a single specimen. Its coloration is produced by varying combinations of trace elements such as iron, manganese, chromium, vanadium, copper, lithium, and others within the crystal structure. Fine specimens may exhibit exceptional transparency, vivid coloration, strong pleochroism, or striking internal zoning. Exceptional crystals may be preserved in their natural elongated prismatic form for collectors, scholars, temples, or arcane displays. Tourmaline is frequently mounted in gold, platinum, silver, electrum, bronze, copper, or elaborate settings and is especially suited to ornaments depicting elemental symbols, dragons, serpents, stars, forests, oceans, flames, storms, and other motifs associated with the forces of nature and the mysteries of creation.

In many cultures, tourmaline is associated with balance, transformation, protection, creativity, elemental harmony, and the infinite variety of the natural world. homebrew.name: Meteoric Iron Nugget
homebrew.desc:
Meteoric Iron Nugget

A meteoric iron nugget is a naturally occurring fragment of iron-rich material originating beyond the world and deposited upon its surface by the fall of a meteorite. Unlike ordinary terrestrial iron ore, meteoric iron is typically composed primarily of iron alloyed with substantial amounts of nickel and smaller quantities of cobalt and other elements. Its coloration ranges from steel gray and silvery gray on freshly exposed surfaces to charcoal, dark brown, or nearly black where weathering has produced an oxidized crust. Natural specimens may be rounded, irregular, pitted, grooved, or deeply sculpted by intense heating and ablation during their passage through the atmosphere. When cut, polished, and properly treated, some meteoric iron reveals distinctive interlocking crystalline patterns produced by the extremely slow cooling of its metallic structure before reaching the world. Such patterns cannot easily be duplicated in ordinary forged iron and make suitable specimens immediately recognizable to knowledgeable smiths, mineralogists, and natural philosophers.

Smiths, jewelers, collectors, natural philosophers, rulers, and weaponsmiths prize meteoric iron nuggets for their celestial origin, unusual metallic composition, distinctive internal structures, and rarity. Small nuggets may be polished or mounted largely unaltered as pendants, rings, brooches, amulets, seals, cloak fasteners, holy symbols, or ceremonial ornaments, while larger specimens may be preserved as curiosities, temple relics, royal treasures, or scholarly objects. Particularly fine pieces may be sliced and polished to display their internal crystalline patterns, which can then be incorporated into jewelry, weapon fittings, plaques, boxes, and decorative inlays. Larger masses may instead be forged, often with considerable difficulty, into blades, arrowheads, spearheads, tools, or ceremonial weapons whose material literally descended from the heavens. Specimens possessing substantial size, unusual natural sculpting, a well-preserved dark fusion crust, high metallic content, prominent internal crystalline patterns, or a reliably documented fall are particularly desirable. homebrew.unid:
Nugget

A nugget is a naturally occurring piece of native metal or other valuable material found as a discrete lump rather than extracted from ordinary mineral ore. Nuggets are most famously associated with gold, but native silver, copper, platinum, electrum, and other metals may also occur in irregular masses worthy of collection or ornamental use. Their shapes range from flattened flakes and rounded pebbles to knobby lumps, branching masses, and jagged crystalline forms, depending upon how they formed and whether they were transported by water. Their coloration, weight, luster, and resistance to tarnish depend upon their composition, with precious-metal nuggets often possessing a distinctive density that immediately distinguishes them from ordinary stones of similar size.

Jewelers, miners, collectors, merchants, and metalworkers prize nuggets for their precious-metal content as well as for unusual natural shapes that can make individual specimens valuable beyond the worth of the material itself. Less remarkable specimens are commonly weighed and valued primarily for their metal content before being melted into coinage, jewelry, ingots, or crafted objects. Natural nuggets are especially popular among dwarven jewelers and metalworkers, who may design settings around the original contours of a particularly impressive specimen rather than reshaping it into a conventional ornament.

In many cultures, nuggets are associated with prosperity, discovery, good fortune, opportunity, abundance, and wealth drawn directly from the earth. Miners, prospectors, merchants, travelers, dwarven clans, frontier communities, and adventurers sometimes preserve the first valuable nugget recovered from a new mine or expedition as a token of future success. Large or unusually shaped specimens may acquire individual names and histories, becoming family heirlooms, guild trophies, temple offerings, or symbols of ownership over productive mines and territories. Dwarven traditions may regard an exceptional natural nugget as a particularly pure expression of the earth's wealth, especially when precious metal remains intertwined with the stone in which it formed. Prospectors may carry tiny nuggets as good-luck charms, while rulers and merchant princes may display enormous specimens as demonstrations of the mineral wealth under their control. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though nuggets are favored components for enchanted items concerned with earth, metal, prosperity, luck, finding treasure, locating mineral deposits, or revealing valuables concealed beneath the ground.

homebrew.name: Pale Blue Kyanite
homebrew.desc:
Pale Blue Kyanite

Pale blue kyanite is an elegant variety of kyanite distinguished by delicate blue coloration and the elongated, bladelike crystal forms characteristic of the mineral. Natural specimens commonly form flattened blades or elongated crystals marked by pronounced lengthwise striations, and some occur as radiating or overlapping formations resembling feathers, icicles, spearheads, or slender sword blades. Fine specimens may be transparent to translucent and possess a bright glassy to pearly luster, with lighter-colored crystals sometimes displaying a particularly luminous appearance. Kyanite possesses markedly different hardness depending upon the direction in which it is tested, making its crystals challenging to cut and polish without splitting. When expertly worked, pale blue kyanite can produce delicate gemstones with a cool brilliance reminiscent of clear morning skies or sunlight reflected from ice.

Particularly attractive natural crystals may be preserved largely unaltered and incorporated into pendants, ritual ornaments, mineral displays, or jewelry designed to emphasize their elongated form. Specimens possessing clear pale blue coloration, good transparency, strong surface luster, sharply defined blades, substantial size, minimal fractures, or attractive variations between icy and deeper blue are particularly desirable. Pale blue kyanite is frequently mounted in silver, platinum, electrum, white gold, or pale yellow gold and is especially suited to ornaments depicting feathers, icicles, stars, clouds, waves, swords, and other motifs associated with clarity, sky, water, and precise direction.

In many cultures, pale blue kyanite is associated with clarity, tranquility, guidance, truth, patience, and focused purpose. homebrew.name: Pale Green Jade

Jewelers and ornamental carvers prize pale green jade for its delicate coloration, exceptional toughness, smooth texture, and extraordinary suitability for detailed carving. Specimens possessing delicate but clearly perceptible green coloration, strong translucency, uniform fine texture, substantial size, minimal fractures, or especially graceful transitions between white and green are particularly desirable. Jade's exceptional toughness allows skilled artisans to produce thin pierced designs, intricate reliefs, and finely detailed carvings that would be hazardous in many more brittle gemstones. Pale green jade is frequently mounted in silver, platinum, electrum, pale gold, or carved wooden settings and is especially suited to ornaments depicting leaves, blossoms, birds, butterflies, clouds, young trees, and other motifs associated with nature, renewal, serenity, and growth.
