homebrew.name: Black Moldavite
homebrew.desc:
Black Moldavite

Black moldavite is an exceptionally dark form of moldavite, a natural impact glass created when the tremendous heat and pressure of an ancient meteorite impact melted terrestrial material and hurled it through the atmosphere before it cooled and fell back to the earth. Its coloration ranges from extremely dark olive and brownish green to green-black and nearly opaque black, with thinner edges or strongly illuminated portions often revealing the deep green or brown-green coloration concealed within the glass. Natural specimens commonly possess deeply sculpted, wrinkled, pitted, grooved, or irregular surfaces produced by their formation and subsequent weathering, giving them an appearance reminiscent of cooled slag, charred glass, twisted flames, or strangely shaped fragments of dark stone. Fine specimens may contain bubbles, flowing internal structures, wispy inclusions, or translucent zones visible when held before a powerful light. When carefully cut and polished, black moldavite develops a bright glassy luster that contrasts dramatically with the rugged texture of an unworked specimen.

Jewelers, collectors, natural philosophers, and ornamental carvers prize black moldavite for its unusually dark coloration, extraterrestrial association, distinctive natural sculpting, and rarity. Particularly attractive natural specimens are often preserved largely unaltered as curiosities, amulets, pendants, scholarly specimens, or ceremonial objects, since extensive cutting removes the characteristic surface textures that demonstrate the material's unusual history. Suitable pieces may nevertheless be polished or faceted for pendants, rings, earrings, brooches, seals, and other prestigious ornaments, especially when thinner portions reveal green beneath the nearly black exterior. Specimens possessing exceptionally dark coloration, dramatic natural sculpting, unusual shapes, substantial size, minimal damage, or contrasting translucent green edges and internal structures are particularly desirable. Black moldavite is frequently mounted in silver, platinum, electrum, gold, iron, or darkened metal and is especially suited to ornaments depicting stars, comets, eclipses, flames, dragons, eyes, and other motifs associated with celestial catastrophe, darkness, transformation, and extraordinary events.

In many cultures, black moldavite is associated with transformation, celestial power, catastrophe, mystery, endurance, and forces arriving from beyond the familiar world. Astrologers, diviners, priests, wizards, natural philosophers, collectors, nobles, and adventurers sometimes prize black moldavite as tangible evidence of the tremendous forces unleashed when the heavens strike the earth. Its nearly black appearance may inspire darker legends than those surrounding ordinary green moldavite, with some traditions describing it as celestial fire extinguished within the earth, fragments of fallen stars burned black during their descent, or glass formed where a divine weapon struck the mortal world. Wizards and diviners may value specimens whose hidden green translucence becomes visible only under intense light as symbols of concealed knowledge or power, while dwarven scholars may admire the material as evidence that forces greater than any ordinary forge can transform stone into glass almost instantaneously. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though black moldavite is a favored material for enchanted items concerned with transformation, divination, celestial phenomena, fire, darkness, planar travel, teleportation, or protection against dangers originating beyond the mortal world.

homebrew.name: Black Pearl
homebrew.desc:
Black Pearl

Black pearls are rare and highly prized organic gemstones formed within saltwater oysters and distinguished by their dark coloration, exceptional luster, and exotic beauty. Unlike minerals formed through geological processes, pearls are created through biological activity as the oyster deposits successive layers of nacre around an irritant or implanted nucleus. Their colors range from charcoal and smoky gray to deep black, black-green, peacock, blue-black, violet-black, and dark silver, often displaying subtle overtones of green, purple, bronze, blue, or rose that shift beneath changing light. The finest specimens possess a deep reflective luster known as orient, created by the interaction of light with thousands of microscopic nacre layers. Black pearls may occur in perfectly round, near-round, oval, drop, button, or irregular baroque forms, with exceptionally large or uniquely shaped examples commanding great admiration. homebrew.name: Greenish-Blue Aquamarine
homebrew.desc:
Greenish-Blue Aquamarine

Greenish-blue aquamarine is a luminous and highly admired variety of aquamarine distinguished by the mingling of cool blue with subtle sea-green coloration. Its hues range from pale turquoise and watery blue-green to deeper shades reminiscent of clear coastal seas, sheltered lagoons, and sunlit ocean depths. The finest specimens display an even balance of blue and green throughout the crystal, creating a harmonious coloration that captures both the serenity of the sea and the vitality of living waters. When expertly faceted and polished, greenish-blue aquamarine develops a brilliant glassy luster, producing shifting flashes of blue, green, and silver as it catches the light, much like sunlight reflecting across moving waves.

homebrew.name: Kunzite
homebrew.desc:
Kunzite

Kunzite is a transparent to translucent gemstone variety of spodumene renowned for its delicate pink to violet coloration and bright glassy luster. Its hues range from nearly colorless blush pink and pale rose to lilac, lavender-pink, violet-pink, and occasionally rich purplish pink, with strongly saturated specimens being particularly desirable. Kunzite displays pronounced pleochroism, causing its apparent color and intensity to change when viewed from different directions, and skilled gemcutters orient stones to display their strongest and most attractive pink or violet hues. Natural crystals may grow to impressive sizes and commonly exhibit lengthwise striations, while gem-quality material can possess exceptional transparency. When expertly faceted and polished, kunzite develops lively brilliance and soft flashes of pink, lavender, and violet that give fine stones a luminous and elegant appearance.

Jewelers prize kunzite for its graceful coloration, excellent transparency, availability in comparatively large clear crystals, and distinctive directional color changes. Transparent gem-quality material is commonly faceted for pendants, necklaces, earrings, brooches, circlets, tiaras, rings, and ceremonial jewelry, although its perfect cleavage requires care when cutting, setting, or wearing the stone. Translucent or heavily included material may be fashioned into cabochons, beads, amulets, seals, and small carvings. Specimens possessing vivid pink or violet-pink coloration, excellent transparency, substantial size, strong pleochroism, and minimal disruptive inclusions are particularly valuable. Kunzite is frequently mounted in silver, platinum, electrum, white gold, or pale yellow gold and is especially suited to ornaments depicting flowers, hearts, butterflies, stars, moons, and other motifs associated with beauty, affection, refinement, and gentle light.

In many cultures, kunzite is associated with affection, compassion, serenity, devotion, emotional clarity, and enduring friendship. Lovers, nobles, diplomats, healers, priests, artists, elven jewelers, and wealthy adventurers sometimes wear kunzite as a symbol of affection expressed with sincerity and restraint rather than uncontrolled passion. Its delicate pink and violet coloration may cause courtly traditions to favor it for betrothal gifts, friendship tokens, reconciliation offerings, and jewelry commemorating important personal bonds. Elven artisans may particularly admire transparent lavender-pink specimens for ornaments celebrating twilight blossoms, courtship, or peaceful companionship, while philosophers may interpret the stone's changing coloration when viewed from different directions as a reminder that understanding another person often requires seeing circumstances from more than one perspective. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though kunzite is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with healing, friendship, diplomacy, protection, mental clarity, emotional influence, or resistance to fear and despair.

homebrew.name: Leaf Green Moldavite

Leaf green moldavite is an attractive variety of moldavite distinguished by fresh, natural green coloration reminiscent of young foliage. Like other moldavite, it is a natural impact glass formed when the tremendous heat and pressure of an ancient meteorite impact melted terrestrial material and hurled it through the atmosphere, where it cooled into glass before falling back to the earth. Its hues range from pale yellow-green and spring green to fresh leaf green, olive-green, and moderately deep forest green, sometimes displaying subtle golden, brown, or yellow undertones. Natural specimens commonly possess deeply sculpted, wrinkled, pitted, or grooved surfaces produced by their formation and subsequent weathering, often resembling leaves, bark, flames, or irregular fragments of translucent glass. Fine material is transparent to translucent and may contain bubbles, flowing internal structures, wispy inclusions, or variations in color created as the molten glass cooled. When carefully faceted or polished, leaf green moldavite develops a bright glassy luster and a luminous green interior that contrasts dramatically with its rugged natural surface.

Jewelers, collectors, natural philosophers, and ornamental carvers prize leaf green moldavite for its appealing coloration, unusual impact origin, distinctive natural sculpting, and rarity. Particularly attractive natural specimens are often preserved largely unaltered as curiosities, amulets, pendants, scholarly specimens, or ceremonial objects, since extensive cutting destroys the characteristic surface textures that reveal the material's unusual history. Transparent gem-quality pieces may nevertheless be carefully faceted for rings, pendants, earrings, brooches, circlets, and other prestigious jewelry, while thicker translucent material may be polished into cabochons, beads, seals, or small carvings. Specimens possessing vivid leaf-green coloration, strong transparency, dramatic natural sculpting, substantial size, minimal damage, or especially attractive internal bubbles and flow structures are particularly desirable. Leaf green moldavite is frequently mounted in gold, silver, platinum, electrum, bronze, or carved wooden settings and is especially suited to ornaments depicting leaves, trees, stars, comets, flames, dragons, and other motifs associated with nature, celestial phenomena, transformation, and renewal.

In many cultures, leaf green moldavite is associated with transformation, renewal, celestial power, vitality, revelation, and the meeting of heaven and the living earth. White danburite is a luminous variety of danburite distinguished by shades of snowy white, ivory, pearl, and silvery white coloration. Its appearance ranges from nearly transparent to softly translucent, with some specimens containing delicate internal veils, cloudy areas, or faint colorless zones that scatter light throughout the crystal. Fine gem-quality stones possess exceptional clarity and a cool white radiance, producing brilliant flashes of silver and white as they are turned beneath the light. When expertly faceted and polished, white danburite develops a bright glassy luster that gives the gemstone a clean, elegant appearance reminiscent of frost, crystalline ice, or freshly fallen snow.

Jewelers, artisans, collectors, and craftsmen value white danburite for its clarity, brilliance, refined coloration, and graceful appearance. Transparent specimens are commonly faceted into gemstones for rings, pendants, earrings, brooches, circlets, crowns, and ceremonial jewelry, while translucent or larger crystals may be fashioned into cabochons, amulets, seals, decorative inlays, devotional objects, and ornamental carvings. Specimens possessing luminous white coloration, exceptional transparency, strong brilliance, and minimal inclusions are particularly desirable. White danburite is frequently mounted in silver, platinum, electrum, or pale gold and is especially suited to ornaments depicting stars, rays, feathers, doves, halos, and other motifs associated with purity, illumination, protection, and celestial grace.

In many cultures, white danburite is associated with purity, wisdom, spiritual clarity, divine illumination, protection, and truth unclouded by deception. Priests, scholars, healers, diviners, and contemplatives sometimes carry polished stones as symbols of clear intentions, disciplined thought, and the pursuit of understanding free from worldly distractions. Some religious traditions incorporate particularly luminous specimens into sacred objects representing enlightenment, divine wisdom, and the purity of celestial realms, while philosophers may regard the gemstone's pale radiance as a symbol of the mind made clear through reflection and study. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though white danburite is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with purification, mental clarity, spiritual protection, revelation, or the detection of illusions and deception.

Danburite

Jewelers, artisans, collectors, and craftsmen value danburite for its clarity, brilliance, durability, and elegant appearance. homebrew.name: Black Opal
homebrew.desc:
Black Opal

Black opal is one of the rarest and most highly prized varieties of opal, distinguished by its dark body color and vivid flashes of play-of-color that appear to glow against a deep background. Unlike crystalline gemstones, opal is a hydrated form of silica composed of microscopic silica spheres arranged in patterns that can diffract light into brilliant displays of color. Its body coloration ranges from dark gray and charcoal to deep brown, black, and nearly midnight black, with the darkest specimens providing the greatest contrast for their internal flashes. The play-of-color may include brilliant red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, and multicolored patterns, with red flashes being especially valued due to their rarity. Fine black opals may display broad patches of color, pinfire patterns, rolling flashes, harlequin-like arrangements, or complex scenes resembling galaxies, flames, oceans, or magical lights suspended within darkness. When expertly cut and polished, black opal develops a smooth waxy to glassy luster and an extraordinary depth that makes its colors appear to float within the stone.

Jewelers and ornamental carvers prize black opal above most other opal varieties for its rarity, dramatic contrast, and spectacular color effects. Fine material is commonly fashioned into cabochons, pendants, earrings, rings, brooches, amulets, seals, circlets, and ceremonial jewelry, while exceptional specimens may be preserved as collector gems or incorporated into royal treasures and magical artifacts. Cabochon cutting is preferred because the rounded surface allows the play-of-color to move and change as the stone is viewed from different angles. Specimens possessing intense red flashes, broad multicolored fire, a deep dark body tone, unusual patterns, strong brilliance, substantial size, or minimal flaws are particularly desirable. Black opal is frequently mounted in silver, platinum, electrum, white gold, yellow gold, or darkened metal and is especially suited to ornaments depicting eclipses, dragons, ravens, stars, flames, galaxies, eyes, oceans, and other motifs associated with mystery, darkness, magic, and hidden wonders.

In many cultures, black opal is associated with prophecy, hidden knowledge, transformation, mystery, imagination, and the power of unseen forces. Wizards, diviners, sorcerers, priests, nobles, artists, elven artisans, and adventurers sometimes carry black opal as a symbol of truths concealed within darkness and visions revealed only to those capable of understanding them. Its brilliant colors emerging from a shadowy background may inspire legends that it contains fragments of distant stars, trapped lightning, the dreams of ancient creatures, or glimpses of other realms hidden within the world. Diviners may prize stones displaying unusual patterns as windows into possible futures, while illusionists may favor the gem because its shifting colors resemble the unstable nature of appearances and perception. Elven traditions may regard black opals with deep blue, violet, and green flashes as reflections of twilight realms or forgotten celestial places, while darker cultures may associate them with secrets, hidden power, and forbidden knowledge. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though black opal is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with illusions, divination, prophecy, transformation, dreams, shadow, planar mysteries, or the revelation of hidden truths.
homebrew.unid:
Opal

Opal is a unique gemstone renowned for its shifting play of color, delicate translucence, and remarkable variety of appearances. Unlike most gemstones, opal is not a crystalline mineral but a hydrated form of silica composed of microscopic silica spheres arranged in varying patterns. When these spheres are regularly arranged, they can diffract light and produce flashes of spectral color known as play-of-color, with displays of blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and violet appearing as the stone is moved beneath the light. Opal varieties may range from transparent and colorless to opaque white, gray, black, brown, or vividly colored, with some specimens displaying broad flashes of multiple colors while others show only subtle internal shimmer. Fine opals possess a smooth waxy to glassy luster and a luminous depth that can make their colors appear to float within the stone rather than merely reflect from its surface.

Jewelers and ornamental carvers prize opal for its extraordinary color effects, individuality, and dreamlike appearance. Fine material is commonly fashioned into cabochons, beads, pendants, earrings, brooches, rings, amulets, seals, gaming pieces, and decorative inlays, while larger specimens may be carved into figurines, plaques, boxes, small vessels, and ceremonial objects. Cabochon cutting is especially favored because a rounded polished surface allows the play-of-color to spread across the stone and shift dramatically as it moves. Exceptional specimens possessing vivid red flashes, broad areas of multicolored fire, strong contrast, high transparency, unusual patterns, substantial size, or rare body colors are particularly desirable. Opal is frequently mounted in silver, gold, platinum, electrum, bronze, or delicate settings that protect the relatively soft stone and allow light to enter from multiple directions. It is especially suited to ornaments depicting rainbows, stars, eyes, flames, oceans, flowers, dragons, and other motifs associated with wonder, magic, dreams, and hidden beauty.

In many cultures, opal is associated with inspiration, prophecy, imagination, transformation, hope, and the mysterious forces of creation. Artists, bards, diviners, sorcerers, priests, nobles, and adventurers sometimes carry opal as a symbol of visions, creativity, and possibilities not yet revealed. Some traditions regard opal as a fortunate stone that grants insight and imagination, while others treat it with caution because its ever-changing appearance is associated with uncertainty, illusion, and forces beyond mortal understanding. homebrew.name: Black Star Sapphire
homebrew.desc:
Black Star Sapphire

Black star sapphire is a rare and striking variety of corundum distinguished by its deep black, charcoal, dark gray, and nearly opaque body coloration combined with a remarkable star-like optical effect known as asterism. The star phenomenon is created by microscopic needle-like inclusions, typically of rutile or related minerals, that reflect light in intersecting patterns across the surface of the polished stone. Fine specimens display a sharp, centered star that appears to glide across the surface as the gemstone is moved beneath a light source. When carefully polished as a cabochon, black star sapphire develops a smooth glassy luster that enhances its dark depth and reveals a luminous six-rayed star that seems suspended within the stone.

Jewelers, collectors, nobles, and artisans prize black star sapphire for its exceptional hardness, durability, rarity, and dramatic optical effect. It is almost exclusively cut as a cabochon, since faceting would diminish the visibility of the star, and is commonly fashioned into rings, pendants, brooches, amulets, signet stones, ceremonial ornaments, and prestigious talismans. Specimens possessing a sharply defined star, strong contrast between the bright rays and dark body, smooth surface, substantial size, and rich black coloration are particularly desirable. Black star sapphire is frequently mounted in silver, platinum, white gold, electrum, or darkened metals and is especially suited to ornaments depicting eyes, eclipses, ravens, wolves, dragons, shields, crowns, and other motifs associated with vigilance, mystery, protection, and authority.

In many cultures, black star sapphire is associated with protection, foresight, discipline, endurance, hidden knowledge, and unwavering resolve. Warriors, rulers, scouts, guardians, and adventurers sometimes carry polished stones as symbols of vigilance and the ability to perceive dangers concealed in darkness. Some traditions regard the moving star within the gemstone as a watchful celestial eye that never closes, while others interpret the dark surface and shining star as a reminder that wisdom and hope may exist even within the most difficult circumstances. Diviners may value particularly fine specimens as symbols of insight, destiny, and the ability to recognize paths hidden from ordinary perception.

Dwarven traditions often esteem black star sapphire as one of the most impressive treasures of the deep earth, believing its dark body represents the ancient mountains while its internal star reflects the hidden fires and forces that shaped them. Some dwarven clans associate especially large specimens with legendary guardians, forgotten vaults, and ancestral protections placed upon great treasures. Arcane scholars may interpret the gemstone as a symbol of focused power concealed beneath a calm exterior, representing discipline, patience, and mastery over unseen forces. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though black star sapphire is a favored gemstone for enchanted items concerned with protection, perception, divination, darkness, mental fortitude, vigilance, resistance to deception, or the detection of hidden threats.

Diamond is an exceptionally hard and brilliant gemstone prized for its extraordinary durability, transparency, and ability to scatter light into vivid flashes of color. Most gem-quality diamonds are colorless or nearly so, though natural specimens may also occur in shades of yellow, brown, blue, green, pink, red, gray, and black. Fine colorless stones possess remarkable clarity and an adamantine luster unmatched by most other gemstones, while internal inclusions may appear as tiny crystals, wisps, clouds, or minute fractures that provide each stone with a unique character. When expertly faceted and polished, diamond reflects and refracts light with intense brilliance, producing sharp flashes of white light and spectral color that can make a finely cut stone appear to shine from within.

Jewelers, artisans, collectors, and craftsmen prize diamond for its exceptional hardness, brilliance, rarity, and enduring beauty. Gem-quality crystals are commonly faceted into gemstones for rings, necklaces, earrings, brooches, circlets, crowns, ceremonial regalia, and other prestigious jewelry, while lesser stones may be employed by skilled artisans for engraving, cutting, or polishing exceptionally hard materials. Specimens possessing exceptional clarity, strong brilliance, desirable coloration, and substantial size are particularly valuable. Diamonds are frequently mounted in platinum, gold, electrum, or silver and are especially suited to ornaments depicting stars, crowns, suns, shields, swords, and other motifs associated with permanence, authority, protection, and power.

In many cultures, diamond is associated with strength, purity, invincibility, wealth, constancy, endurance, and enduring authority. Rulers, nobles, champions, priests, and wealthy merchants sometimes wear diamonds as symbols of unbreakable resolve, lasting oaths, and elevated status, while warriors may regard the gemstone's legendary hardness as an emblem of courage, discipline, and the refusal to yield under pressure. Dwarven traditions often esteem diamonds as supreme examples of treasures created through immense pressure in the deepest reaches of the earth, representing patience, resilience, and the hidden wonders forged by the mountains themselves. Some religious traditions employ flawless diamonds as symbols of incorruptible truth, divine perfection, or the eternal nature of the soul. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though diamond is a favored gemstone for powerful enchanted items concerned with protection, durability, light, purity, resistance to destructive forces, the strengthening of magical barriers, or the enhancement and focusing of magical power.

homebrew.name: Smoky Diamond
homebrew.desc:
Smoky Diamond

Smoky diamond is an uncommon and distinctive variety of diamond distinguished by shades of pale smoke, taupe, gray-brown, deep brownish gray, and dark charcoal coloration. Its subdued hues may result from natural irradiation, structural irregularities, or minute inclusions within the crystal and can range from a faint smoky tint to a deep, shadowy coloration approaching black. Fine specimens retain excellent transparency despite their darker appearance, while others contain minute crystalline inclusions, wispy clouds, or tiny internal fractures that add depth and character. When expertly faceted and polished, smoky diamond displays an intense adamantine luster and extraordinary brilliance, producing sharp flashes of silver, bronze, brown, white, and spectral color that seem to emerge from within its shadowed interior.

Jewelers, artisans, collectors, and nobles prize smoky diamond for its exceptional hardness, unusual coloration, brilliance, and sophisticated appearance. Gem-quality crystals are commonly faceted into gemstones for rings, necklaces, earrings, brooches, circlets, crowns, signet ornaments, ceremonial regalia, and other prestigious jewelry, while especially large or unusually dark specimens may become centerpieces of noble collections or royal treasures. Stones possessing exceptional clarity, an even smoky coloration, substantial size, and superior brilliance are particularly valuable. Smoky diamonds are frequently mounted in platinum, silver, gold, electrum, or darkened metal and are especially suited to ornaments depicting mountains, wolves, ravens, dragons, eclipses, towers, and other motifs associated with endurance, mystery, hidden strength, and the unseen depths of the world.

In many cultures, smoky diamond is associated with resilience, secrecy, steadfastness, protection, hidden strength, and endurance through adversity. Rulers, warriors, scouts, dwarven nobles, and wealthy adventurers sometimes wear smoky diamonds as symbols of unwavering resolve and the ability to withstand hardship without revealing weakness. Dwarven traditions may regard their shadowed transparency and extraordinary hardness as embodiments of the deepest mountain stone, where ancient pressures create treasures that endure beyond the memory of living creatures. Some mystical traditions associate their smoky interiors with safe passage through darkness, uncertainty, and hidden dangers, believing the gemstone represents strength that does not need to announce itself to be effective. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though smoky diamond is a favored gemstone for powerful enchanted items concerned with protection, darkness, earth, durability, concealment, resilience, or resistance to destructive forces.

homebrew.name: Violet Diamond
homebrew.desc:
Violet Diamond

Violet diamond is an exceptionally rare and highly prized variety of diamond distinguished by shades of pale lavender-violet, rich violet, blue-violet, and deep purple-violet coloration. Its hues result from unusual structural characteristics and trace impurities within the crystal and may range from a delicate violet tint to an intense, evenly saturated color. Fine specimens possess exceptional transparency and clarity, though natural stones may contain minute crystalline inclusions, wispy clouds, or tiny internal fractures that contribute to their individuality. When expertly faceted and polished, violet diamond displays an intense adamantine luster and extraordinary brilliance, producing sharp flashes of violet, blue, purple, white, and spectral color that give the gemstone a luminous and almost otherworldly appearance.

Jewelers, artisans, collectors, and rulers prize violet diamond for its exceptional hardness, extraordinary rarity, brilliance, and distinctive coloration. Gem-quality crystals are commonly faceted into gemstones for rings, necklaces, earrings, brooches, circlets, crowns, ceremonial regalia, and other prestigious jewelry, while large or intensely colored specimens may become legendary treasures associated with royal houses, temples, archmages, or ancient hoards. Stones possessing exceptional clarity, strong and evenly distributed violet coloration, substantial size, and superior brilliance are particularly valuable. Violet diamonds are frequently mounted in platinum, silver, gold, or electrum and are especially suited to ornaments depicting stars, crowns, eyes, moons, dragons, spirals, and other motifs associated with mystical knowledge, authority, revelation, and hidden power.

In many cultures, violet diamond is associated with arcane power, spiritual insight, wisdom, prophecy, perception, and indomitable strength of mind. Archmages, diviners, high priests, rulers, and renowned adventurers sometimes wear violet diamonds as symbols of extraordinary awareness and mastery over forces beyond ordinary understanding. Arcane traditions may regard the combination of ethereal violet coloration and extraordinary hardness as an emblem of disciplined magical power, representing knowledge and ability refined through years of study and practice. Diviners sometimes consider exceptionally clear specimens symbols of truths that remain immutable despite changing circumstances, while philosophers may associate the gemstone with the pursuit of wisdom beyond the limits of common perception. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though violet diamond is a favored gemstone for powerful enchanted items concerned with divination, arcane magic, mental fortitude, protection, durability, resistance to enchantment, or defense against destructive forces.

homebrew.name: Yellow Diamond
homebrew.desc:
Yellow Diamond

Yellow diamond is an exceptionally rare and highly prized variety of diamond distinguished by shades of pale lemon, canary yellow, golden yellow, and deep amber-yellow coloration. Its color results primarily from trace amounts of nitrogen incorporated into the crystal during its formation and may range from a faint yellow tint to an intense, evenly saturated golden hue. Fine specimens possess exceptional transparency and clarity, though natural stones may contain minute crystalline inclusions, wispy clouds, or tiny internal fractures that contribute to their individuality. When expertly faceted and polished, yellow diamond displays an intense adamantine luster and extraordinary brilliance, producing sharp flashes of yellow, gold, white, and spectral color that give the gemstone an appearance reminiscent of concentrated sunlight captured within crystal.

Jewelers, artisans, collectors, and rulers prize yellow diamond for its exceptional hardness, rarity, brilliance, and radiant coloration. Gem-quality crystals are commonly faceted into gemstones for rings, necklaces, earrings, brooches, circlets, crowns, ceremonial regalia, and other prestigious jewelry, while large or intensely colored specimens may become famous treasures associated with royal houses, temples, or legendary hoards. Stones possessing exceptional clarity, strong and evenly distributed yellow coloration, substantial size, and superior brilliance are particularly valuable. Yellow diamonds are frequently mounted in gold, platinum, electrum, or silver and are especially suited to ornaments depicting suns, crowns, lions, stars, coins, halos, and other motifs associated with light, prosperity, authority, and divine favor.

In many cultures, yellow diamond is associated with prosperity, confidence, sovereignty, enlightenment, wisdom, and enduring good fortune. Rulers, wealthy merchants, high priests, guildmasters, and renowned adventurers sometimes wear yellow diamonds as symbols of lasting wealth and authority strengthened by discipline, insight, and determination. Agricultural cultures may associate their brilliant golden coloration with the life-giving sun and abundant harvests, viewing especially vivid specimens as emblems of fertility and seasonal renewal. Dwarven traditions may regard yellow diamonds as supreme manifestations of golden light captured within the hardest treasures of the deep earth, representing both the wealth hidden beneath the mountains and the skill required to uncover it. These beliefs do not necessarily indicate magical properties, though yellow diamond is a favored gemstone for powerful enchanted items concerned with prosperity, sunlight, protection, confidence, leadership, durability, or resistance to darkness and destructive forces.
